article_content:
How Codex runs commands on your machine with limits you control.

At OpenAI, we take a defense in depth⁠(opens in a new window) approach when it comes to safeguarding agents. While our investments in training and alignment are fundamental to this effort, we also implement features in our agentic harness, Codex⁠(opens in a new window), to provide additional protections. Because one of the most common (and potentially risky) things Codex does is run commands on your computer, we built the Codex sandbox so Codex can work in your existing environment within filesystem and network limits you control.

A ⁠(opens in a new window)sandbox⁠(opens in a new window) limits what a program can access while it runs. For a photo-organizing task, you might configure the Codex sandbox to let commands read and modify files in ~/Pictures while blocking network access to prevent uploads. For code review, you might allow access to online documentation while keeping source files read-only. Users configure the Codex sandbox through ⁠(opens in a new window)permission profiles⁠(opens in a new window), which define the filesystem and network restrictions for a Codex session.

In this article, we’ll start with the tradeoffs behind Codex’s sandbox defaults, then explain the sandbox’s design and how the harness uses it to run commands. We’ll show how end users and enterprises can tailor its permissions to their needs and how developers can reuse the sandbox in their own tools. Finally, we’ll examine how these restrictions are enforced on macOS, Linux, and Windows.

In Codex, our philosophy is to specify conservative defaults for the sandbox that still enable meaningful work. For example, with a Git repository as the workspace root, the built-in :workspace permission profile:

Allows writes within the workspace, while keeping directories such as .git and .codex read-only. This lets Codex edit source code without seeking permission for every change, while preventing direct changes to .codex/config.toml or Git hooks under .git/hooks.

Allows broad filesystem reads, subject to the user’s existing OS permissions. Compilers, runtimes, and build tools depend on SDKs, libraries, and configuration outside the repository. Restricting reads to the workspace would break many ordinary workflows. The tradeoff is that sensitive files elsewhere on the machine may also remain readable (such as config files containing API keys).

Disables network access. This blocks direct uploads to external services, including attempts to exfiltrate data the command can read. It also prevents legitimate operations such as downloading dependencies, which require additional access.

These restrictions prevent a large class of bad behavior, but harmful actions are still possible. For example, the agent could inject malicious code into a locally installed package such as node_modules/prettier. Such a change might not appear in git status because node_modules is often ignored by Git. If the user’s editor runs that copy of Prettier on save, simply saving a file could execute the malicious code outside the Codex sandbox. This is why we take a defense in depth approach: the sandbox limits what commands can access, while training and alignment help the model use that access in accordance with the user’s intent.

For guidance on tailoring sandbox permissions and combining them with other protections in an enterprise environment, see the Codex security cookbook⁠(opens in a new window).

Virtual machines and containers⁠(opens in a new window) are two popular mechanisms used for sandboxing, but we take a different approach with the Codex sandbox. Instead of moving computation to a separate environment to provide isolation, Codex uses each platform’s sandboxing facilities to constrain commands running in the user’s existing environment.For many developers, their laptop serves as a bespoke dev environment that they can change on a whim. Reproducing that environment in a Docker container can take work, and some workflows still depend on tools that run on the host.

For example, consider using Codex to develop an iOS app on a Mac. If you decided to sandbox Codex by running it inside Docker, Codex would not be able to run the iOS build toolchain composed of native Mac executables, nor could it launch the iPhone simulator to run the code. A Docker-based workflow could delegate builds and simulator operations to the Mac host, but those operations would execute outside the container’s sandbox and would need their own restrictions. For Codex, we prefer to keep things simple by investing heavily in OS-specific sandboxing so Codex can run in the environment that is most appropriate to the task at hand.

The harness exposes these OS-specific sandboxing mechanisms through a common API across macOS, Windows, and Linux. This API takes a command and a permission profile. If the permission profile allows limited network access, the caller must supply a network proxy to enforce those limits:

1# This is a simplified version of the actual API.2def spawn_command_under_sandbox(3 program_and_args: list[str],4 cwd: Path,5 env: dict[str, str],6 permission_profile: PermissionProfile,7 network_proxy: NetworkProxy | None,8) -> Child:This function starts the process in a sandbox and returns a Child handle the harness can use to wait for it to finish. Each child process inherits its parent’s sandbox constraints, so those restrictions apply throughout the process tree initiated by the command, even to descendants that outlive the original process.

The following diagram shows how these pieces fit together, from configuration to running a sandboxed command. The sections that follow explain each stage.

How the harness leverages the sandboxAs explained in Unrolling the Codex Agent Loop, the Codex harness is responsible for executing tool calls generated by the model. For coding tasks, the most commonly used tool is a shell tool, which runs commands much as a user would in an interactive shell such as Bash. Here we’ll examine the one-shot ⁠(opens in a new window)exec_command⁠(opens in a new window) shell tool⁠(opens in a new window) to illustrate how the harness employs the sandbox to achieve the desired protections.This is a simplified version of how the exec_command tool call would be honored by the Codex harness without sandboxing:

1# Illustrative implementation of the exec_command tool call.23class ExecCommandToolCall:4 cmd: str5 workdir: str | None = None6 shell: str | None = None7 login: bool = True8 timeout_ms: int = 10_00091011def perform_exec_command(tool_call: ExecCommandToolCall):12 program_and_args = [13 tool_call.shell or os.environ.get("SHELL") or "/bin/sh",14 "-lc" if tool_call.login else "-c",15 tool_call.cmd,16 ]17 child = subprocess.Popen(18 program_and_args,19 # workdir defaults to the turn's cwd, assumed here to be the process cwd.20 cwd=Path(tool_call.workdir or ".").absolute(),21 stdout=subprocess.PIPE,22 stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,23 )24 output, exit_code = collect_output(child, timeout_ms=tool_call.timeout_ms)25 return {"output": output, "exit_code": exit_code}To sandbox the command, the harness replaces the call to subprocess.Popen() with spawn_command_under_sandbox(). The harness supplies the permission profile and, when needed, the network proxy:

1# Honoring the exec_command tool call while enforcing sandbox constraints.23def perform_exec_command_with_sandboxing(4 tool_call: ExecCommandToolCall,5 permission_profile: PermissionProfile,6 network_proxy: NetworkProxy | None,7):8 # ...build program_and_args as in the previous example...9 child = spawn_command_under_sandbox(10 program_and_args=program_and_args,11 cwd=Path(tool_call.workdir or ".").absolute(),12 env=os.environ.copy(),13 permission_profile=permission_profile,14 network_proxy=network_proxy,15 )16 output, exit_code = collect_output(child, timeout_ms=tool_call.timeout_ms)17 return {"output": output, "exit_code": exit_code}The exec_command tool also lets the model request different permissions for an individual command, but the harness decides whether to grant the request:

1class ExecCommandToolCall:2 # ...command-related fields...34 # Per-command sandbox override. Defaults to "use_default".5 sandbox_permissions: Literal[6 "use_default",7 "with_additional_permissions",8 "require_escalated",9 ] = "use_default"1011 # User-facing approval question; only for "require_escalated".12 justification: str | None = None1314 # Expand network or filesystem access; only for "with_additional_permissions".15 # AdditionalPermissions supports fine-grained options.16 additional_permissions: AdditionalPermissions | None = NoneWhen use_default is specified, the harness uses the default sandbox config for the turn. with_additional_permissions requests expanded access within the sandbox, while require_escalated requests execution outside it. The harness evaluates the request based on the user’s preferences before executing the command. (For example, Codex may prompt the user directly, or it might route the request to auto-review⁠(opens in a new window).) If execution is authorized, Codex will pass the appropriate permission_profile and network_proxy to perform_exec_command_with_sandboxing() with the command arguments from the original ExecCommandToolCall.

The shell tool is the primary consumer of spawn_command_under_sandbox(), and the harness also reuses its sandboxing infrastructure for operations such as reading and modifying local files. This reuse extends beyond the harness: the codex sandbox command lets you incorporate sandboxed command execution into your own tools, as we’ll see later. Next, we’ll look at how permission profiles are defined.

A named permission profile lets you reuse the same filesystem and network restrictions across projects. You can define your own profiles under [permissions] in config.toml. For example, the following defines a profile named dev that extends⁠(opens in a new window) the built-in :workspace profile:

1# Use the dev profile by default.2default_permissions = "dev"34[permissions.dev]5# This is displayed when /permissions is run in the Codex CLI.6description = "Development with extra read-only protections."78# A profile can be derived from an existing profile.9# Profiles starting with ":" are provided by Codex.10extends = ":workspace"1112[permissions.dev.filesystem]13"~/build-cache" = "write"1415[permissions.dev.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]16".devcontainer" = "read"17".vscode" = "read"18"**/*.env" = "deny"19"secrets" = "deny"The dev profile adds write access to ~/build-cache and places additional restrictions on files in the workspace. Filesystem entries can grant read-only access (read), grant read and write access (write), or block access entirely (deny).

The :workspace_roots table lets you define rules for paths relative to a project’s workspace roots. By default, the Codex CLI uses its working directory as its sole workspace root, while the ChatGPT desktop app uses the project’s source folders. Codex applies each rule to every root, so the .vscode entry in dev makes the .vscode directory read-only under each root.

1[permissions.":workspace".filesystem.":workspace_roots"]2".agents" = "read"3".aws" = "read"4".codex" = "read"5".git" = "read"Network permissionsWhen it comes to configuring the network for the sandbox in Codex, there are roughly three options:

To give dev direct network access, set permissions.dev.network.enabled = true at the top level of config.toml. This grants full network access when the network proxy is disabled.

1[permissions.dev.network]2enabled = true34[permissions.dev.network.domains]5"*.openai.com" = "allow"6# Allow requests to local services by hostname or by IPv4/IPv6 loopback address.7"localhost" = "allow"8"127.0.0.1" = "allow"9"::1" = "allow"10"evil.example" = "deny"1112[features]13# If neither local config nor managed requirements enable the proxy,14# this profile allows direct network access; domain rules are not enforced.15network_proxy = trueDomain rules support exact names and wildcard patterns, with explicit deny rules taking precedence over allow rules. Requests to other domains require approval or are blocked, as described in Network proxy below.

Individual users can configure defaults that apply across projects and override them for a particular trusted project. Enterprise administrators may also want to configure defaults for their users and constrain which settings those users can change. Codex supports both through layered configuration and managed requirements.

As described in Configuration precedence,⁠(opens in a new window) Codex merges settings from multiple config.toml files. Tables are merged recursively, with the higher-precedence source winning when values conflict. Arrays are replaced as a whole.

This is why permission profiles use tables for filesystem paths and network domains. A team can add or override individual entries in its own configuration and automatically inherit changes to all other entries in the organization’s base configuration:

1[permissions.dev.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]2".idea" = "read"34[permissions.dev.network.domains]5"example.com" = "allow"Administrators can also supply managed requirements⁠(opens in a new window) through requirements.toml to constrain users’ configuration choices. These requirements can come from multiple sources, including system files and cloud-provided policy. A common use case is to specify allowed_permission_profiles to constrain the set of permission profiles an enterprise user can select. For example, an administrator could specify these cloud requirements:

1default_permissions = ":read-only"23[allowed_permission_profiles]4":read-only" = true5":danger-full-access" = falseThe cloud requirements would take precedence over the system requirements file at /etc/codex/requirements.toml, so an entry in that file cannot override the explicit ":danger-full-access" = false above. Leaving :workspace unspecified allows another requirements layer to supply that entry. Profiles whose entries are false or absent from the final merged table are unavailable.This separation lets organizations enforce limits while users tailor their configuration within those limits. The resulting permission profiles can be used by the harness or applied directly to a command, as we’ll see next.

The Codex CLI provides a sandbox command to facilitate running an arbitrary command under a permission profile defined in the Codex config. This is commonly used to test out the profile, ensuring that the sandbox prevents the behavior it was designed to block.

For example, the following command attempts to configure VS Code to run a malicious auto-formatter on save. Assuming .vscode already exists, the dev profile defined above should block this write because that directory is read-only (codex sandbox treats cwd as a workspace root by default):

1codex sandbox --permission-profile dev -- \2 bash -c 'cat > .vscode/settings.json' <<'JSON'3{4 "prettier.prettierPath": "./node_modules/evil-prettier",5 "[typescript]": {6 "editor.defaultFormatter": "esbenp.prettier-vscode",7 "editor.formatOnSave": true8 }9}10JSONIndeed, on macOS this fails with:

1bash: .vscode/settings.json: Operation not permittedThe codex sandbox command makes Codex’s sandboxing mechanism available independently of an agent session. You can use the same configuration language and platform-specific enforcement to constrain commands launched by your own tools.

For a stdio MCP server configured in config.toml, the Codex harness does not attempt to sandbox the command used to start the server. Codex cannot reliably infer which files or network services that server needs, so applying a default sandbox profile could break an otherwise valid configuration.

1[mcp_servers.memory]2command = "npx"3args = [4 "-y",5 "@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory@1.0.0"6]78[mcp_servers.memory.env]9MEMORY_FILE_PATH = "~/mcp-data/memory.jsonl"Because this npx command runs unsandboxed, it can write files and make network requests with the same permissions as the user running Codex, which is overly permissive. To lock it down, we can define a permission profile named memory-mcp and then wrap the original npx command with codex sandbox --permission-profile memory-mcp to limit where the server can write and to prevent it from accessing the network:

1[permissions.memory-mcp.filesystem]2# Allow broad reads for Node.js/npm dependencies and configuration.3":root" = "read"4"~/.npm" = "write"5"~/mcp-data" = "write"67[permissions.memory-mcp.network]8enabled = false910[mcp_servers.memory]11command = "codex"12args = [13 "sandbox",14 "--permission-profile",15 "memory-mcp",16 "--",17 "npx",18 "--offline",19 "@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory@1.0.0"20]2122[mcp_servers.memory.env]23MEMORY_FILE_PATH = "~/mcp-data/memory.jsonl"Before starting the server, create its data directory and populate the npm cache with the pinned package. That lets npx --offline launch the server under a profile that disables network access:

1# The sandbox can write to this folder, but it cannot create it.2mkdir -p ~/mcp-data34# Installing the MCP server requires network access.5npx -y --package=@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory@1.0.0 -c trueOnce the package is cached, Codex can start the memory server without network access, with writes limited to the npm cache and the server’s data directory.

The sandbox implementation turns a permission profile into restrictions enforced by the operating system. The network proxy’s core request-handling and policy logic is shared across all three major operating systems, while proxy setup and integration with the sandbox are OS-specific. We’ll examine the shared proxy first, followed by the implementations for macOS, Linux, and Windows.

To enforce a permission profile’s network restrictions, the harness starts a network proxy and configures the sandbox to allow connections to it while blocking direct connections to external hosts. The proxy checks each request against the profile’s domain rules to determine whether to forward it.

In the Codex repo, the network proxy is implemented in the codex-network-proxy⁠(opens in a new window) crate, which the harness uses as a library, though it can also be built as a standalone CLI⁠(opens in a new window). When enabled, codex-network-proxy starts both an HTTP proxy and a SOCKS5 proxy by default. These proxy addresses are communicated to the process spawned by the sandbox via environment variables. In addition to injecting standard environment variables such as HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, and ALL_PROXY, a number of well-known application-specific environment variables⁠(opens in a new window) (such as PIP_PROXY) are injected, as well. Admittedly, not all programs honor these environment variables. If a program attempts a direct connection to an external host, the operating system’s sandbox restrictions block it, as described in the platform-specific sections below.

The network proxy is responsible for implementing the network restrictions defined in a permission profile. For example, the dev profile shown earlier allows requests to *.openai.com and explicitly denies requests to evil.example. When a request targets a domain that does not match an allow or deny rule, the proxy can suspend the request while it delegates to the harness for approval. Like the shell command example, Codex may prompt the user directly, or it might route the request to auto-review⁠(opens in a new window). Upon receiving a decision, the proxy either allows the request to proceed or rejects it with an error response.

The order matters here because even a DNS lookup can leak information encoded in a hostname. The proxy therefore resolves the requested hostname only after determining that it is allowed or approved. Note that broad wildcard rules or access to DNS services can still permit DNS-based exfiltration.

On macOS, Codex uses Seatbelt⁠(opens in a new window), Apple’s kernel-enforced sandboxing mechanism. Seatbelt policies are written in Sandbox Profile Language (SBPL), a Scheme-based language for expressing sandbox restrictions. Codex invokes Seatbelt through macOS’s /usr/bin/sandbox-exec command. Like codex sandbox, it takes options describing the sandbox followed by the command to run:

1sandbox-exec -p PROFILE [-Dkey=value]* -- PROG ARGS...The PROFILE is a string of SBPL that contains entries that configure the sandbox. For example, the following SBPL snippet makes /dev/null and /dev/zero readable and writable under the sandbox policy:

1; local HTTP proxy launched by Codex2(allow network-outbound (remote ip "localhost:3128"))34; local SOCKS proxy launched by Codex5(allow network-outbound (remote ip "localhost:8081"))Codex’s base profile starts with (deny default), so outbound connections remain blocked unless explicitly allowed.

1; Pass -DWRITABLE_ROOT_0=/path/to/dir to specify a folder that cannot be removed.2(deny file-write-unlink3 (require-all4 (literal (param "WRITABLE_ROOT_0"))5 (vnode-type DIRECTORY)))which are populated by the -Dkey=value options passed to sandbox-exec.

To implement its own sandbox API, Codex builds up the list of arguments⁠(opens in a new window) to sandbox-exec starting from a base policy⁠(opens in a new window), and then uses permission_profile and other context to amend it to produce the complete Seatbelt profile. The resulting profile and accompanying -D arguments configure the restrictions enforced by Seatbelt, while the network proxy enforces additional network rules. With the full arg list assembled, the invocation of sandbox-exec is straightforward.

Generating the correct SBPL is challenging because Apple does not document the language for third-party use. Indeed, man sandbox-exec states The sandbox-exec command is DEPRECATED (as is the sandbox_init() library function documented via man 3 sandbox_init). Despite the deprecation warning, macOS still ships Seatbelt profiles in /usr/share/sandbox, and third-party software, including Google Chrome and Chromium⁠(opens in a new window), continues to rely on Seatbelt. As such, we plan to continue to use Seatbelt for the foreseeable future.

To create the sandbox on Linux, Codex uses a combination of bubblewrap⁠(opens in a new window) (bwrap), a command-line tool for constructing isolated environments, and seccomp-bpf⁠(opens in a new window), a Linux kernel mechanism for filtering system calls. An internal helper named codex-linux-sandbox coordinates the setup. Like sandbox-exec on macOS, it takes a sandbox configuration followed by a command to run:

1codex-linux-sandbox SANDBOX_ARGS... -- PROG ARGS...When filesystem isolation or proxy routing is required, codex-linux-sandbox invokes bwrap to create the initial sandbox environment. bwrap then launches codex-linux-sandbox --apply-seccomp-then-exec inside it. This second invocation uses seccomp-bpf to apply additional restrictions before running the user’s command.

To construct that initial sandbox environment, Codex uses bubblewrap to create a filesystem view in a separate mount namespace that reflects the permission profile’s filesystem rules. Because this is fundamental to the sandbox implementation, Codex vendors its own copy of bwrap in case the user has not installed their own, but it prefers a compatible installation of ⁠(opens in a new window)bwrap⁠(opens in a new window) found on PATH, when available. Empirically, some Linux distributions disable access to user namespaces by default⁠(opens in a new window), but grant an exception for the system bwrap.

Also like sandbox-exec, bwrap takes a sandbox configuration followed by a command to run within the sandbox. Instead of using a custom config language like SBPL, bwrap uses individual flags for configuration. Codex uses the following options to create the filesystem view:

To apply deny globs using these options, Codex expands them to concrete paths before launching each command. New matching paths are not automatically added to that command’s sandbox restrictions.

Codex also specifies options such as --unshare-ipc and --unshare-pid to prevent the sandbox from accessing other types of resources on the host, so bubblewrap affects more than just file visibility.

When using bubblewrap, Codex passes --unshare-net whenever networking is disabled or connections must go through the network proxy, which will create a new network namespace for the sandbox. We then use seccomp-bpf to apply additional restrictions on the networking system calls and socket families available to the command.

Specifically, we use the seccompiler crate⁠(opens in a new window) to dynamically compile a BPF program based on the desired filters⁠(opens in a new window) and apply it to a launcher process in the sandbox so the constraints are inherited by the entire process tree. As such, bwrap does not run the user’s command, but runs the codex-linux-sandbox launcher with its own config args followed by the user’s command:

1bwrap BWRAP_ARGS......

article_content_zh:
Codex 如何在您的机器上运行命令并限制您的控制。

在 OpenAI，我们在保护代理方面采取深度防御⁠（在新窗口中打开）方法。虽然我们在培训和协调方面的投资是这项工作的基础，但我们还在代理工具 Codex（在新窗口中打开）中实施了功能，以提供额外的保护。由于 Codex 所做的最常见（且有潜在风险）的事情之一是在您的计算机上运行命令，因此我们构建了 Codex 沙箱，以便 Codex 可以在您控制的文件系统和网络限制内的现有环境中工作。

沙盒（在新窗口中打开）限制程序运行时可以访问的内容。对于照片组织任务，您可以配置 Codex 沙箱，让命令读取和修改 ~/Pictures 中的文件，同时阻止网络访问以防止上传。对于代码审查，您可以允许访问在线文档，同时保持源文件只读。用户通过 ⁠(opens in a new window) 权限配置文件 ⁠(opens in a new window) 配置 Codex 沙箱，该配置文件定义了 Codex 会话的文件系统和网络限制。

在本文中，我们将从 Codex 沙箱默认值背后的权衡开始，然后解释沙箱的设计以及工具如何使用它来运行命令。我们将展示最终用户和企业如何根据自己的需求定制其权限，以及开发人员如何在自己的工具中重用沙箱。最后，我们将研究如何在 macOS、Linux 和 Windows 上实施这些限制。

在 Codex 中，我们的理念是为沙箱指定保守的默认值，但仍能实现有意义的工作。例如，使用 Git 存储库作为工作区根目录，内置 :workspace 权限配置文件：

允许在工作区中写入，同时保持 .git 和 .codex 等目录只读。这使得 Codex 可以编辑源代码，而无需每次更改都寻求许可，同时防止直接更改 .codex/config.toml 或 .git/hooks 下的 Git 挂钩。

允许广泛的文件系统读取，但取决于用户现有的操作系​​统权限。编译器、运行时和构建工具依赖于存储库外部的 SDK、库和配置。限制对工作区的读取会破坏许多普通的工作流程。代价是机器上其他地方的敏感文件也可能保持可读（例如包含 API 密钥的配置文件）。

禁用网络访问。这会阻止直接上传到外部服务，包括尝试窃取命令可以读取的数据。它还会阻止合法操作，例如下载依赖项，这需要额外的访问权限。

这些限制可以防止大量不良行为，但有害行为仍然可能发生。例如，代理可以将恶意代码注入本地安装的包（例如node_modules/prettier）中。这样的更改可能不会出现在 git status 中，因为 node_modules 通常被 Git 忽略。如果用户的编辑器在保存时运行该 Prettier 副本，则只需保存文件就可以在 Codex 沙箱之外执行恶意代码。这就是我们采取深度防御方法的原因：沙箱限制可以访问的命令，而训练和对齐帮助模型根据用户的意图使用该访问权限。

有关定制沙箱权限并将其与企业环境中的其他保护相结合的指南，请参阅 Codex 安全指南⁠（在新窗口中打开）。

虚拟机和容器⁠（在新窗口中打开）是用于沙箱的两种流行机制，但我们对 Codex 沙箱采取了不同的方法。 Codex 没有将计算转移到单独的环境中以提供隔离，而是使用每个平台的沙箱设施来限制在用户现有环境中运行的命令。对于许多开发人员来说，他们的笔记本电脑充当定制的开发环境，他们可以随意更改。在 Docker 容器中复制该环境可能需要一些工作，并且某些工作流程仍然依赖于主机上运行的工具。

例如，考虑使用 Codex 在 Mac 上开发 iOS 应用程序。如果您决定通过在 Docker 中运行 Codex 来对 Codex 进行沙箱处理，Codex 将无法运行由本机 Mac 可执行文件组成的 iOS 构建工具链，也无法启动 iPhone 模拟器来运行代码。基于 Docker 的工作流程可以将构建和模拟器操作委托给 Mac 主机，但这些操作将在容器的沙箱之外执行，并且需要它们自己的限制。对于 Codex，我们更愿意通过大力投资特定于操作系统的沙箱来让事情变得简单，以便 Codex 可以在最适合手头任务的环境中运行。

该工具通过跨 macOS、Windows 和 Linux 的通用 API 公开这些特定于操作系统的沙箱机制。该 API 采用命令和权限配置文件。如果权限配置文件允许有限的网络访问，调用者必须提供网络代理来强制实施这些限制：

1# 这是实际 API 的简化版本。2defspawn_command_under_sandbox(3program_and_args:list[str],4cwd:Path,5env:dict[str,str],6permission_profile:PermissionProfile,7network_proxy:NetworkProxy|None,8)->Child:此函数在沙箱中启动进程并返回一个子句柄，安全带可以使用它来等待它完成。每个子进程都会继承其父进程的沙箱约束，因此这些限制适用于命令启动的整个进程树，甚至适用于比原始进程寿命更长的后代。

title: Anthropic IPO set to deliver windfall to handful of smaller VC firms
title_en: Anthropic IPO set to deliver windfall to handful of smaller VC firms

inline_images.caption: Manager of pop superstar Madonna, Guy Oseary, stands to net more than $7bn from an early investment of just over $400mn © Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg
inline_images.alt: Manager of pop superstar Madonna, Guy Oseary, stands to net more than $7bn from an early investment of just over $400mn © Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg

author: George Hammond
article_content:
Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday will reorder Silicon Valley’s power rankings, with a small group of venture capitalists who bet early and aggressively on the AI lab set for a combined windfall of well over $100bn.

Anthropic is expected to be valued at $1.4tn or more when it lists. That would be about 2,300 times its value when Anjney Midha — an angel investor and founder of AMP PBC — first backed the company in 2021.

His firm is among a handful of lesser-known groups primed for massive returns at multiples that would surpass those of larger, blue-chip rivals. Others include Spark Capital, which would own about $11bn of stock at a $1.4tn valuation, and Factorial Funds, which would own just over $10bn, according to FT calculations.

Spark’s Yasmin Razavi and Factorial’s Sol Bier invested in Anthropic’s series C funding round, which closed in 2023, when the company was valued at about $4bn. Razavi sits on Anthropic’s board.

“The deck chairs are shifting around in the VC landscape,” said a partner at one midsized VC firm which stands to make billions of dollars. “The leaders in the AI wave are not the same as they were in the previous waves. Different firms are moving up the leaderboard, and we’re glad to be among them.”

Amazon and Google, which have provided investment and computing resources to Anthropic, will collectively own close to 30 per cent of the company after the IPO.

The largest financial investor in the company, Iconiq Capital, holds a fraction of that. Nevertheless, its stake would be worth about $28bn at a $1.4tn valuation. It is followed by Lightspeed Ventures — which has invested roughly $3.2bn for a stake worth just over $25bn at the same valuation — and Menlo Ventures, which stands to return $21bn from an initial $1bn investment.

Coatue and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC invested later but went big. The pair led a funding round earlier this year which valued Anthropic at $380bn, and have each put close to $5bn into the company. Those stakes would be worth more than $10bn at an IPO price of $1.4tn.

Sound Ventures, which was founded by Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, and Bessemer Venture Partners are each poised for returns of about $7bn. For Bessemer, that would mark an eightfold increase on its initial investment, while Sound stands to make roughly 17 times its outlay.

Even those massive multiples are dwarfed, though, by the roughly 70-times return jailed crypto exchange founder Sam Bankman-Fried would have made if his company had not been forced to sell its $500mn stake in bankruptcy proceedings in 2024. That stake would be worth about $35bn at an IPO price of $1.4tn.

The clamour to own a stake in the AI company has increased in the past year, as the group’s revenues have leapfrogged rival OpenAI. A partner at one of Anthropic’s large investors said they “wrote [chief financial officer Krishna Rao] a love letter” as they jostled for access to a funding round earlier this year.

The take-off prompted OpenAI’s investors, including Brad Gerstner’s Altimeter, Sequoia Capital and Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund, to pour money into Anthropic, an unusual move in Silicon Valley, where VCs tend to back a single company in each field and founders prize fealty.

Other big-name venture firms, including Thrive Capital and Andreessen Horowitz, skipped Anthropic entirely.

“Call us old school . . . but we are serial monogamists,” said Josh Kushner, founder of Thrive, which is one of OpenAI’s largest and most vocal backers, in a since-deleted post on X.

Andreessen’s partners and Anthropic’s executives, meanwhile, have clashed over how best to regulate AI.

A successful IPO would also make thousands of Anthropic employees multimillionaires.

However, the company’s executives have framed fundraising as a necessary evil in the pursuit of their mission to responsibly “develop advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity”.

While its investors celebrate once-in-a-lifetime returns, Anthropic’s leadership is plotting a low-key IPO. The company has no plans for a party to celebrate the listing and intends to keep fanfare around what is set to be the biggest listing fundraise of all time to a minimum, said people with knowledge of the matter.
content_snippet: Small group of lesser-known firms primed for returns at multiples that would surpass larger, blue-chip rivals.
summary_en: AI startup Anthropic is preparing for its IPO with an expected valuation of $1.4 trillion, set to deliver over $100 billion in combined returns to early-stage venture capital firms including Spark Capital and Factorial Funds. Post-IPO, Amazon and Google will collectively control nearly 30% of the company, while major investors like Iconiq Capital, Lightspeed Ventures, and Menlo Ventures see their stakes reach multi-billion dollar valuations.
title_zh: Anthropic启动IPO，VC市场权力格局重塑
summary_zh: Anthropic计划上市，预估市值达1.4万亿美元，将导致早期风投机构获得千亿美元级回报，并改变硅谷创投权力排行榜
article_content_zh:
Anthropic 周四的首次公开募股将重新调整硅谷的实力排名，一小群早期积极押注人工智能实验室的风险投资家预计将获得远远超过 1000 亿美元的意外之财。

Anthropic 上市时预计估值为 1.4 兆美元或更高。这将是天使投资人兼 AMP PBC 创始人 Anjney Midha 于 2021 年首次支持该公司时市值的 2,300 倍。

他的公司是少数几家鲜为人知的集团之一，它们的回报倍数将超过规模更大的蓝筹竞争对手。根据英国《金融时报》的计算，其他公司包括 Spark Capital 和 Factorial Funds，前者将以 1.4 万亿美元的估值持有约 110 亿美元的股票，后者将持有略高于 100 亿美元的股票。

Spark 的 Yasmin Razavi 和 Factorial 的 Sol Bier 投资了 Anthropic 的 C 轮融资，该轮融资于 2023 年结束，当时该公司估值约为 40 亿美元。 Razavi 是 Anthropic 的董事会成员。

与此同时，流行巨星麦当娜的经纪人 Guy Oseary 有望从刚刚超过 4 亿美元的早期投资中净赚超过 70 亿美元。

“风投领域的躺椅正在发生变化，”一家中型风投公司的合伙人表示，该公司有望赚取数十亿美元。 “人工智能浪潮中的领导者与之前浪潮中的领导者不同。不同的公司正在排行榜上攀升，我们很高兴成为其中之一。”

为 Anthropic 提供投资和计算资源的亚马逊和谷歌在 IPO 后将共同持有该公司近 30% 的股份。

该公司最大的金融投资者 Iconiq Capital 持有其中的一小部分。尽管如此，按 1.4 万亿美元的估值计算，其股份价值约为 280 亿美元。紧随其后的是 Lightspeed Ventures（该公司已投资约 32 亿美元，以相同估值购买了价值略高于 250 亿美元的股份）和 Menlo Ventures（该公司将从最初 10 亿美元的投资中获得 210 亿美元的回报）。

Coatue 和新加坡主权财富基金 GIC 后来投资，但规模很大。今年早些时候，两人领投了一轮融资，对 Anthropic 的估值为 3800 亿美元，并各自向该公司投资了近 50 亿美元。按 1.4 万亿美元的 IPO 价格计算，这些股份的价值将超过 100 亿美元。

由 Oseary 和演员阿什顿·库彻 (Ashton Kutcher) 创立的 Sound Ventures 和 Bessemer Venture Partners 预计将获得约 70 亿美元的回报。对于 Bessemer 来说，这意味着其初始投资增加了 8 倍，而 Sound 的支出将增加约 17 倍。

不过，如果他的公司没有在 2024 年破产程序中被迫出售其 5 亿美元的股份，那么与被监禁的加密货币交易所创始人 Sam Bankman-Fried 获得的大约 70 倍的回报相比，即使是这些巨大的倍数也显得相形见绌。按 1.4 万亿美元的 IPO 价格计算，这些股份的价值约为 350 亿美元。

去年，随着该集团的收入超越了竞争对手 OpenAI，入股这家人工智能公司股份的呼声越来越高。 Anthropic 的一位大型投资者的合伙人表示，他们在今年早些时候争夺一轮融资时“写了一封情书”。

这一腾飞促使 OpenAI 的投资者，包括布拉德·格斯特纳 (Brad Gerstner) 的 Altimeter、红杉资本 (Sequoia Capital) 和彼得·泰尔 (Peter Thiel) 的创始人基金 (Peter Thiel) 等创始人基金，向 Anthropic 注入资金，这在硅谷是一个不寻常的举动，在硅谷，风投倾向于支持每个领域的一家公司，并且创始人会高度忠诚。

其他知名风险投资公司，包括 Thrive Capital 和 Andreessen Horowitz，完全跳过了 Anthropic。

title: Managing frontier AI risk: From training to deployment
title_en: Managing frontier AI risk: From training to deployment

inline_images.caption: Securing our frontier model training environment — Cover
inline_images.alt: Securing our frontier model training environment — Cover

inline_images.caption: How we detect frontier model misalignment — Cover
inline_images.alt: How we detect frontier model misalignment — Cover

inline_images.caption: Our framework for reporting model misalignment — card image
inline_images.alt: Our framework for reporting model misalignment — card image

author: OpenAI
article_content:
The capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating, and our ability to understand, align, and secure them must stay ahead. We are pacing the development and release of our models, including pausing internal training⁠(opens in a new window) or holding back models like GPT‑6.1 Astra when we need more time to meet our safety standards. We’ve introduced new processes such as safety cases and require stronger evidence of aligned behavior throughout training. These requirements slow the pace of model releases, but they give us greater confidence to safely move forward.

Since the Hugging Face incident⁠ in July, we've strengthened safeguards and alignment requirements for how we train, test, and deploy models. This post explains how we evaluate and manage risk at each stage, from highly sandboxed training environments to the Codex deployment you use on your computer. We evaluate both models and safeguards at each stage, requiring a safety review to advance to the next stage.

We use defense in depth with multiple layers of protection that reduce dependence on any single safeguard. If one layer fails, others help prevent harm, limit consequences, or alert us so we can intervene.

Effective monitoring depends on model monitorability - how reliably monitors can detect mistakes or unsafe behavior from a model’s reasoning and actions. For example, a model that verbalizes its intention to cheat in its chain-of-thought (CoT) is more monitorable than one that omits this information. We evaluate monitorability during training and before deployment, develop better methods for measuring⁠(opens in a new window) it, and study what affects it⁠(opens in a new window).

The Hugging Face incident showed why we should not rely on sandboxing alone to contain highly capable models. We now monitor frontier models across most internal and external deployment settings, including all internal deployments that use tools.

Research: We train, test, and use models in sandboxed environments.

Internal deployment: OpenAI employees use models for practical work.

External deployment: Models become available to people and organizations more broadly.

We rely on different layers at different stages. During training, when alignment is less certain, we depend more heavily on sandboxing and monitoring. As models gain broader access during deployment, alignment and system-level controls become increasingly important. At each stage, we evaluate whether the combined protections are sufficient for the model’s capabilities and access. Our determinations may be reviewed with our Safety Advisory Group (SAG) and overseen by the Safety and Security Committee (SSC) of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board of Directors.

During the research phase, we evaluate models to gain confidence in their alignment properties. Because we cannot yet fully rely on alignment to prevent harm, we rely heavily on security and sandboxing to restrict what they can access and do.

Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no live internet access. After the Hugging Face incident, we significantly restructured our internal research systems to contain models using:

We continuously red-team this system, having teams of our strongest models try to reach the live internet, escape security boundaries, or communicate with agents they are meant to be isolated from. This helps us test whether containment holds against the capabilities of the models it is intended to constrain.

As an additional layer of defense, we monitor all frontier inference to detect if the model has bypassed our security invariants. If our monitoring detects that the model has reached the internet, we page our security teams and autopause the workload.

Monitoring provides a critical backstop when containment fails. In a recent misalignment report, we shared that monitors detected an internal research model exploiting a DNS misconfiguration⁠(opens in a new window) to gain limited internet access. We paused training and evaluation of our most capable models from September 20th to October 1st while we investigated and addressed the security gap.

To make interventions fast and reliable, we built Control Room⁠, a central system that tracks research workloads and stops further model output within 35 seconds of receiving an instruction to halt a job. These controls are enforced directly in the inference infrastructure, so they do not depend on each research workload implementing its own shutdown mechanism. For frontier-model research workloads, they also stop model output if Control Room becomes unavailable.

Red-teaming and monitoring work together. We cannot guarantee that a sandbox is impenetrable, but red-teaming helps us assess how much effort a model would need to escape it. The more effort the model requires, the more the opportunity for monitors to detect and stop it.

Models are still being evaluated. Some have not yet completed the safety training, alignment audits, and reviews required for public release.

Frontier research settings can amplify risks. Certain research tasks require more ambitious setups, making the model more persistent or capable than typically seen during external deployment (for example, a team of 10,000 agents was required to solve the Navier Stokes problem).

Training runs at scale with less direct human oversight. Unlike a typical Codex session, our training workloads involve large numbers of model actions without a person following each interaction.

Before broad release, employees switch from sandboxed research use of frontier models to unsandboxed internal use, e.g. making the model accessible in ChatGPT to employees. This gives us a better understanding of how the models behave in practical settings⁠(opens in a new window), and informs deployment decisions.

During this phase, we give the model access to the broader internet, our Slack, our codebase, and internal infrastructure. This is a significant change in risk, as the model’s actions now have a direct impact on the systems we use to build and run OpenAI. During internal deployment, we need to rely more on model alignment, system safeguards, and monitoring as opposed to security controls.

Before a frontier model can be deployed outside of the sandbox, it must first go through alignment and monitorability testing⁠(opens in a new window). We have a suite of alignment evaluations, which test both for specific alignment failure modes (such as circumventing safety and security restrictions) and broad measurements of propensity (such as resampling internal Codex trajectories and checking for misalignment). You can see more about our alignment and monitorability evaluations in the latest GPT‑6 Astra system card⁠(opens in a new window).

Mimicking our production setups, we add an additional layer of defense with system-level classifiers, which are designed to protect against frontier harms such as cyberabuse and bioweaponization. We also generally require Auto-Review⁠(opens in a new window) for employees using Codex, which evaluates potentially risk actions and escalates them back to the user.

Finally, we monitor for misaligned behavior on every frontier inference during internal deployment. Since the model now has expanded privileges and access to internal information and systems, risks such as data exfiltration, or sending sensitive data to an unauthorized destination, become especially important to detect. Monitoring also helps us investigate new forms of misalignment⁠(opens in a new window).

Public deployment exposes models to far more users, tasks, and environments, increasing both the scale and variety of risks. At this stage, we also need to protect against potentially malicious actors who purposefully direct the model to perform harm.

Before public release, models and system safeguards must meet our external deployment safety requirements. We assess them through:

Performing a larger suite of alignment and safety evaluations. For our frontier models, this includes performing new rounds of adaptive testing⁠ with our internal automated redteamers to stress-test the robustness of the model. We publish the results of our capability and safety evaluations in our system cards⁠(opens in a new window).

For our most capable models, we also perform testing with third parties to stress-test both our safeguards against misuse and the underlying alignment of our models.

Examining monitoring flags from the internal deployment stage to track any changes in the base model’s underlying alignment.

In addition to our “synchronous” safeguards (such as model safety training and system classifiers), for external deployments we also leverage offline enforcement and investigation. These teams use a combination of scaled agentic investigators and human review to detect and identify potential threat actors, ranging from cyberabuse, bioweaponization, distillation⁠, and misalignment from the model itself. Offline enforcement is especially helpful to gather information across accounts in order to build a more holistic picture of a potential threat.

Trusted access programs, such as Daybreak and Rosalind⁠, offer another layer of security, and accelerate defenders and legitimate researchers while restricting access by potential attackers.

When we notice a failure in one of our layers of safety, regardless of whether any harm actually occurred, we want to quickly investigate, triage, and if possible and appropriate, disclose the failure externally. Under our misalignment reporting⁠ policy, any employee can flag an incident for public disclosure. These reports are investigated, and if there is a disagreement on whether they should be externally disclosed, the decision is escalated to our Safety Advisory Group (SAG). In addition to relying on employee reports, we proactively look for misalignment incidents so we can address them and share findings.

You can see our misalignment reports here⁠(opens in a new window).

This work depends on both research progress and operational discipline: configuring controls correctly, testing how they interact, and responding decisively when they fail. A misconfigured network service or a failed automatic stop can undermine otherwise strong protections.

As models gain new capabilities, we will need to keep challenging the assumptions behind our safeguards and improving them where necessary. Lessons from research, internal use, and public deployment must inform how we train, evaluate, and deploy the next models.

We will continue sharing findings through system cards, incident reports, internal deployment risk reports⁠(opens in a new window), and external evaluations⁠ so that others can scrutinize our approach, including its limitations. When that evidence falls short of the bar we hold for safety, we will again pause training or withhold release until those requirements are met.

Pacing model development in an era of cyber-critical capabilities — How we slowed frontier training while strengthening containment, expanding monitoring, and requiring stronger evidence of alignment.

Towards safety cases for frontier AI training — Initial guidelines for evidence-based safety arguments covering technical safeguards, operational practices, and investigations of misalignment.

Priorities and principles for effective third party assessments⁠ — Our proposed approach to independent scrutiny of safety cases, safeguards, evaluations, and model behavior.

Periodic Summary of Internal Use Catastrophic-Risk Assessments⁠(opens in a new window) — Our public report covering June–September 2026 describes internal frontier-model deployments, their assessed risks, and changes to safeguards and governance.

An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI⁠ — How we updated the Model Spec around five core values to guide models’ judgment, behavior, and respect for human oversight.

Eval-production behavior gaps in agent safety and the role of eval-awareness⁠(opens in a new window) — A study of differences between safety-evaluation results and production behavior, including how models’ interpretations of evaluation objectives affect performance.

Beyond g-mean²: complementary metrics for monitorability⁠(opens in a new window) — New metrics for comparing monitorability and estimating residual risk in simulated systems where monitors reject model outputs.

GPT‑6 Astra System Card⁠(opens in a new window) — Detailed evaluations of Astra’s capabilities, safety, alignment, and monitorability, alongside its deployment safeguards and limitations.

Training activation classifiers for safety and alignment⁠(opens in a new window) — How classifiers use models’ internal activations to detect potentially harmful behavior and interrupt responses or tool calls.

Auto-review of agent actions without synchronous human oversight⁠(opens in a new window) — How a separate review agent assesses actions that cross sandbox boundaries, helping coding agents work autonomously while blocking potentially harmful or unauthorized actions.

GPT‑Red: Unlocking Self-Improvement for Robustness⁠ — How we train automated red-teamers through self-play to discover vulnerabilities and improve models’ robustness against prompt injections.

Control Room⁠ — How we track workloads across our research infrastructure and enforce rapid stops to model output when safety or security concerns require intervention.

The Hugging Face incident and the road ahead⁠ — Our findings from the Hugging Face incident and the changes it prompted across security, monitoring, and alignment.

An agent used DNS to reach an external chatbot⁠(opens in a new window) — How a research model bypassed internet restrictions through insufficient DNS filtering, how monitoring detected it, and the controls added afterward.

Disrupting a coordinated model-distillation campaign⁠ — How we investigated and disrupted attempts to extract protected model reasoning through account enforcement, technical controls, and partner coordination.

Our framework for reporting model misalignment⁠ — Our process for tracking, investigating, and disclosing concerning model behavior, including cases whose causes or significance remain uncertain.

Misalignment Reports and Notices⁠(opens in a new window) — Our collection of disclosed incidents and notices showing how misalignment arises and where safeguards succeed or fail.

Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI — Early evidence of how coding agents are changing research inside OpenAI, including their growing use, increasingly complex tasks, and effects on experimentation.

On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem — A mathematical proof produced by an internal AI system, accompanied by a Lean formalization, illustrating the capabilities of large-scale research deployments.

Daybreak — Our cybersecurity program provides vetted defenders with advanced AI capabilities, security tools, and support to find vulnerabilities and strengthen defenses.

Introducing GPT‑Rosalind for life sciences research⁠ — A specialized model for biology, drug discovery, and translational medicine, available to eligible organizations through a trusted-access program.
summary_en: The capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating, and our ability to understand, align, and secure them must stay ahead. We are pacing the development and release of our models, including pausing internal training⁠(opens in a new window) or holding back models like GPT‑6.1 Astra when we need more time to meet our safety standards. We’ve introduced new processes such as safety cases and require stronger evidence of aligned behavior throughout training. These requirements slow the pace

article_content_zh:
前沿模型的能力正在迅速增强，我们理解、调整和保护它们的能力必须保持领先。我们正在加快模型的开发和发布速度，包括暂停内部培训⁠（在新窗口中打开）或在需要更多时间来满足安全标准时推迟 GPT-6.1 Astra 等模型。我们引入了安全案例等新流程，并需要更有力的证据来证明整个培训过程中的行为一致。这些要求减缓了模型发布的速度，但它们让我们更有信心安全地前进。

自 7 月份的 Hugging Face 事件以来，我们加强了对训练、测试和部署模型方式的保障措施和一致性要求。这篇文章解释了我们如何评估和管理每个阶段的风险，从高度沙盒的培训环境到您在计算机上使用的 Codex 部署。我们在每个阶段评估模型和保障措施，需要进行安全审查才能进入下一阶段。

我们使用多层保护的深度防御，减少对任何单一防护措施的依赖。如果某一层发生故障，其他层会帮助防止伤害、限制后果或提醒我们以便我们进行干预。

有效的监控取决于模型的可监控性——监控器如何可靠地从模型的推理和操作中检测到​​错误或不安全行为。例如，在思维链 (CoT) 中表达作弊意图的模型比忽略此信息的模型更容易监控。我们在训练期间和部署之前评估可监控性，开发更好的测量方法⁠(在新窗口中打开)，并研究影响它的因素⁠(在新窗口中打开)。

Hugging Face 事件说明了为什么我们不应该仅仅依靠沙箱来包含高性能模型。我们现在监控大多数内部和外部部署设置的前沿模型，包括使用工具的所有内部部署。

研究：我们在沙盒环境中训练、测试和使用模型。

内部部署：OpenAI员工使用模型进行实际工作。

外部部署：模型可供更广泛的人员和组织使用。

我们在不同阶段依赖不同的层。在训练过程中，当对齐不太确定时，我们更加依赖沙箱和监控。随着模型在部署过程中获得更广泛的访问，对齐和系统级控制变得越来越重要。在每个阶段，我们都会评估组合保护是否足以满足模型的功能和访问权限。我们的决定可能会由我们的安全咨询小组 (SAG) 进行审查，并由 OpenAI 基金会董事会的安全和安保委员会 (SSC) 监督。

在研究阶段，我们评估模型以获得对其对齐特性的信心。因为我们还不能完全依靠一致性来防止伤害，所以我们严重依赖安全和沙箱来限制他们可以访问和执行的操作。

根据当前的一致性研究、监控系统和互联网基础设施的安全状况，我们认为负责任的方法是在没有实时互联网接入的情况下进行前沿模型训练。在“抱脸”事件之后，我们对内部研究系统进行了重大重组，以包含使用以下内容的模型：

我们不断地对这个系统进行红队部署，让我们最强大的模型团队尝试访问实时互联网，逃脱安全边界，或者与他们本应隔离的代理进行通信。这有助于我们测试遏制是否符合其旨在约束的模型的功能。

作为额外的防御层，我们监视所有边界推理，以检测模型是否绕过了我们的安全不变量。如果我们的监控检测到该模型已到达互联网，我们就会寻呼我们的安全团队并自动暂停工作负载。

当遏制失败时，监控提供了关键的后盾。在最近的一份错位报告中，我们分享了监视器检测到一个内部研究模型利用 DNS 错误配置⁠（在新窗口中打开）来获得有限的互联网访问权限。从 9 月 20 日到 10 月 1 日，我们暂停了对最有能力的模型的训练和评估，同时调查并解决了安全漏洞。

title: Solana Foundation takes majority stake in crypto data provider CoinGecko
title_en: Solana Foundation takes majority stake in crypto data provider CoinGecko
author: Francisco Rodrigues
content_snippet: The Solana Foundation has taken a majority interest in CoinGecko, one of the crypto ecosystem's most popular price-tracking platforms.
summary_en: The Solana Foundation has secured a majority stake in CoinGecko, a major cryptocurrency data tracking platform with 18 million registered users. This strategic acquisition aims to vertically integrate market data infrastructure to bolster Solana's influence within the DeFi ecosystem's information gateway.

summary_zh: Solana基金会宣布完成对加密货币数据平台CoinGecko的多数股权收购，旨在强化其在Web3信息基础设施领域的控制力

【起因与机理】整合去中心化金融流量入口，加固Solana在区块链生态数据层的竞争优势

article_content_zh:
Solana 基金会持有 CoinGecko 的多数股权，CoinGecko 是加密生态系统中最受欢迎的价格跟踪平台之一。

根据 Solana 基金会的公告，这笔交易可以为 CoinGecko 的 1800 万注册用户带来基于 Solana 的交易。该基金会表示，该平台还通过其数据接口向 180,000 个加密应用程序和企业提供市场数据。

Solana 基金会首席产品官 Vibhu Norby 在社交媒体上透露了多数股权，但双方均未透露购买价格或基金会的确切股权。

CoinDesk 已联系征求意见，但截至撰写本文时尚未收到回复。

该交易于伦敦 Breakpoint 会议上宣布，将专注于扩展 CoinGecko 的市场数据、研究工具和探索交易。

该基金会表示，计划将 Solana 支持的交易引入 CoinGecko 的网站、GeckoTerminal 平台和移动应用程序。诺比还概述了去中心化金融工具以及更广泛的股票和代币化现实世界资产覆盖范围的计划。

CoinGecko 自己的公告将交易描述为一个正在探索的领域。此举可以让用户在不离开 CoinGecko 的情况下研究代币、跟踪价格和进行交易，从而为 Solana 提供了接触加密货币投资者的新方式。

CoinGecko 还计划扩大基于区块链的资产、衍生品和代币化现实世界资产的覆盖范围，同时改善其为企业和金融公司提供的数据服务。

这笔交易是在领先的加密货币交易所 Binance 于 2020 年收购竞争对手加密市场数据提供商 CoinMarketCap 数年后达成的

CoinGecko 表示，它将利用自己的技术和公共数据方法来维持对更广泛的加密货币市场的覆盖。
article_content:
The Solana Foundation has taken a majority interest in CoinGecko, one of the crypto ecosystem’s most popular price-tracking platforms.

The deal could bring Solana-based trading to CoinGecko's 18 million registered users, according to a Solana Foundation announcement. The platform also supplies market data to 180,000 crypto apps and businesses through its data interfaces, the foundation said.

Solana Foundation’s chief product officer, Vibhu Norby, revealed the majority stake on social media, though neither side disclosed the purchase price or the foundation’s exact stake.

CoinDesk has reached out for comments but hasn’t heard back at the time of writing.

The deal, announced at the Breakpoint conference in London, will focus on expanding CoinGecko's market data, research tools and exploring trading.

The foundation said it plans to bring Solana-powered trading to CoinGecko's website, GeckoTerminal platform and mobile app. Norby also outlined plans for decentralized finance tools and broader coverage of stocks and tokenized real-world assets.

CoinGecko's own announcement described trading as an area under exploration. The move could let users research tokens, track prices and place trades without leaving CoinGecko, giving Solana a new way to reach crypto investors.

CoinGecko also plans to expand coverage of blockchain-based assets, derivatives and tokenized real-world assets while improving its data services for businesses and financial firms.

The deal comes years after leading cryptocurrency exchange Binance acquired rival crypto market data provider CoinMarketCap in 2020

CoinGecko said it would maintain coverage of the wider crypto market using its own technology and public data methods.

author: Nick Indge
article_content:
Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company’s vision for its new “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.”

The announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent’s work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.

The rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the company first announced in September. Parts of that vision are now becoming “generally available,” as Nadella puts it, with autonomous agents and new governance tools arriving alongside them.

### All about agents

Copilot Autopilot (not to be confused with Windows Autopilot) is a “persistent, proactive agent for personal productivity” according to Microsoft. In a nutshell, Autopilot is a cloud-based autonomous AI agent that users can delegate responsibilities to, not just single tasks. Autopilot can be authorized to work across services like email and calendars and complete tasks assigned to it as part of its role. Autopilot will use usage-based billing via Copilot Credits, but final pricing has not been announced ahead of general availability.

Also announced as generally available at the keynote speech was Microsoft IQ, an intelligence platform that houses Work IQ, a context layer that helps agents understand a company’s communications, relationships, and ongoing work. Nadella described Work IQ as perhaps a company’s most valuable database: “It has a deep understanding of the people, their relationships to other people, your emails, your meetings, chats, projects that make up all the fabric of work.” Whether companies want autonomous agents to have access to internal documents and messaging data will have to be determined by their own internal IT review.

Copilot Workspaces is a collaborative environment currently available through Microsoft’s Frontier early-access program, but coming soon will be the ability to bring personal Autopilot agents into Workspaces. Early in the keynote address, Nadella said that “Until now, AI interactions have mostly been single-player. Workspaces makes it a truly multiplayer experience, where people and agents drive towards a common goal, with shared context.”

### Governance over trust

Trust, the third pillar of Microsoft’s new frontier ecosystem, was something that Nadella continued returning to during his presentation, and not in a way that some might expect. “We find ourselves in a place where alignment is elusive. Mechanistic understanding of these models is elusive. The question is: How can you even trust all this powerful technology? The reality is, by definition, you can’t,” he said.

In a departure from the norms of “AI is magic” corporate hype sentiment, Nadella conceded that the internal workings of AI thought processes remain difficult to understand, and models cannot be trusted to govern themselves, regardless of whether their answers are accurate. Nadella described the solution as “an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence” from the authority granted to it. Microsoft says each Autopilot agent will have a unique ID, and administrators can restrict permissions or block it entirely. All agent activities are logged for human review, and Autopilot can ask for human approval before engaging in certain actions.

The promised agent controls and admission that AI systems can’t always be trusted are meaningful, but Microsoft is asking businesses and users to place their trust in the company’s own safeguards instead, though the effectiveness of those safeguards against mistakes, rogue actions, or data exposure will still have to be demonstrated. In Microsoft’s view, the solution to untrustworthy intelligence is not to make AI agents trustworthy, but to control what they’re permitted to do. Businesses will have to decide how much autonomy they delegate to agents.

Along with the guardrails, Microsoft announced what it calls the “AI Transparency Initiative.” The effort has partnered with 40-plus major companies, including Adobe and Mastercard, to develop open, industrywide standards for AI governance and security. Nadella described the initiative as a way for industry to “help establish an open standard that makes AI safer, more transparent, and more accessible.”

### Minding and measuring token-spend

Along with the other announced additions, Microsoft also announced expanding capabilities for Agent 365, its existing control plane for managing AI agents across enterprise environments. The new agent sheriff extends existing identity, security, and management systems to AI agents. Microsoft describes the objective as providing “observability at every layer of the stack.” Agent 365 offers governance controls over agent behavior in what Microsoft says is “autonomous in execution, but bounded and supervised.”

Along with Agent 365 comes Agent 365 Business Analytics: “You can simply think of this as an ERP system of AI usage. You can see exactly what’s driving the spend and connect the spend to the outcomes that drive business value,” said Nadella. Customers will be able to see real-world costs associated with AI token-spend, and compare those metrics to the value of work performed. Microsoft acknowledged that the estimations of assisted work hours are determined by a model, and not a direct measurement of time that may have been saved. This is a telling concession for Microsoft to make as businesses evaluate whether there will be an ROI on AI implementations, but according to Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft Commercial Business, “anything you can do with Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot, for less.”

### The outage in the room

Nadella offered only a brief acknowledgment of last week’s outage that disrupted access to services like Exchange Online and Teams for users across the globe. “Last week was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world,” he said. “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously, and in that context I know we have work to do.”

That statement was all the time the elephant in the room was given, but Microsoft did seem to acknowledge the public’s growing concern over data center projects by highlighting the previously discussed “community-first AI infrastructure plan.” Not a surprise in a presentation that asks organizations to extend more autonomy to software agents, at a time when Microsoft’s existing infrastructure is under increased scrutiny.

summary_en: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint within Copilot at Ignite, shifting traditional software apps into secondary plugin components for AI Agents. title_zh: Copilot 是“新的工作操作系统”，现在 Office 在其中运行
summary_zh: 微软在Ignite大会宣布Office三件套深度集成至Copilot，并推出具备自主代理能力的Copilot Autopilot及组织智能平台Work IQ
article_content_zh:
微软首席执行官萨蒂亚·纳德拉在Ignite大会的主旨演讲开场时，阐述了公司对其全新“前沿生态系统”的愿景，并于周二宣布Word、Excel和PowerPoint在Copilot中的正式上线，他将Copilot描述为“全新的工作操作系统”。

这一公告与我们传统上使用软件的方式截然相反。微软设想的新版Copilot集成不再是像Word这样的应用程序成为亮点，而Clippy则作为助手帮助您使用它，而是……

### 关于代理商的一切

根据微软的说法，Copilot Autopilot（不要与 Windows Autopilot 混淆）是“持久、主动的个人生产力代理”。简而言之，Autopilot 是一个基于云的自主人工智能代理，用户可以将职责委派给它，而不仅仅是单个任务。 Autopilot 可以被授权跨电子邮件和日历等服务工作，并完成分配给它的任务，作为其角色的一部分。 Autopilot 将通过 Copilot Credits 使用基于使用情况的计费，但最终定价尚未在全面上市之前公布。

主题演讲中还宣布全面推出 Microsoft IQ，这是一个包含 Work IQ 的智能平台，Work IQ 是一个上下文层，可帮助代理了解公司的通信、关系和正在进行的工作。纳德拉将工作智商描述为也许是公司最有价值的数据库：“它对人、他们与其他人的关系、你的电子邮件、你的会议、聊天、构成工作所有结构的项目有深入的了解。”公司是否希望自主代理能够访问内部文档和消息传递数据必须由他们自己的内部 IT 审查决定。

Copilot Workspaces 是一种协作环境，目前可通过 Microsoft Frontier 早期访问计划获得，但很快就能将个人 Autopilot 代理引入 Workspaces。在主题演讲的早期，纳德拉表示，“到目前为止，人工智能交互大多是单人游戏。工作空间使其成为真正的多人游戏体验，人们和代理在共享背景下朝着共同的目标前进。”

信任是微软新前沿生态系统的第三个支柱，纳德拉在演讲中继续提到这一点，但方式却出乎一些人的预料。 “我们发现自己处于一个难以捉摸的境地。对这些模型的机械理解也难以捉摸。问题是：你怎么能相信所有这些强大的技术？现实是，根据定义，你不能，”他说。

纳德拉与“人工智能是魔法”的企业炒作情绪的规范背道而驰，他承认人工智能思维过程的内部运作仍然难以理解，而且无论模型的答案是否准确，都不能相信模型能够自我管理。纳德拉将该解决方案描述为“将情报供应与授予的权限分开的架构上的必要条件”。微软表示，每个 Autopilot 代理都会有一个唯一的 ID，管理员可以限制权限或完全阻止它。所有代理活动都会被记录下来以供人工审核，并且 Autopilot 可以在执行某些操作之前请求人工批准。

承诺的代理控制和承认人工智能系统并不总是值得信任是有意义的，但微软要求企业和用户转而信任公司自己的防护措施，尽管这些防护措施针对错误、流氓行为或数据泄露的有效性仍需证明。在微软看来，解决不可信情报问题的方法不是让人工智能代理变得值得信赖，而是控制他们被允许做的事情。企业必须决定将多少自主权委托给代理商。

除了护栏之外，微软还宣布了所谓的“人工智能透明度倡议”。该项目已与 Adob​​e 和 Mastercard 等 40 多家大公司合作，为人工智能治理和安全制定开放的全行业标准。纳德拉将该倡议描述为行业“帮助建立开放标准，使人工智能更安全、更透明、更容易获得”的一种方式。

### 关注和衡量代币支出

除了宣布的其他功能外，微软还宣布扩展 Agent 365 的功能，Agent 365 是其现有的控制平面，用于跨企业环境管理 AI 代理。新的特工警长将现有的身份、安全和管理系统扩展到人工智能 智能体。微软将目标描述为“在堆栈的每一层提供可观察性”。 Agent 365 提供对代理行为的治理控制，微软称其“执行自主，但有界和监督”。

与 Agent 365 一起推出的还有 Agent 365 业务分析：“您可以简单地将其视为人工智能使用的 ERP 系统。您可以准确地看到推动支出的因素，并将支出与推动业务价值的结果联系起来。”纳德拉说道。客户将能够看到与人工智能代币支出相关的实际成本，并将这些指标与所执行工作的价值进行比较。微软承认，辅助工作时间的估计是由模型确定的，而不是对可能节省的时间的直接测量。当企业评估人工智能实施是否会带来投资回报时，这是微软做出的一个有说服力的让步，但根据微软商业业务首席执行官 Judson Althoff 的说法，“任何你能用 Claude 或 ChatGPT 做的事情，你都可以用 Copilot 做得更好，而且成本更低。”

纳德拉仅简要承认上周的服务中断，导致全球用户对 Exchange Online 和 Teams 等服务的访问中断。 “上周提醒人们，数字基础设施作为世界的拨号音是多么重要，”他说。 “我们知道您对我们服务的信任，并非常认真地对待这一责任，在这种情况下，我知道我们还有很多工作要做。”

这种说法一直是房间里的大象，但微软确实通过强调之前讨论的“社区优先的人工智能基础设施计划”，似乎承认了公众对数据中心项目日益增长的担忧。在微软现有基础设施受到更严格审查的情况下，要求组织向软件代理提供更多自主权的演讲并不令人意外。

title: Over a Third of Gen Z-ers Rely on AI for Friendship
title_en: Over a Third of Gen Z-ers Rely on AI for Friendship

inline_images.caption: Person sitting looking out of a window while in a silhouette of two people taking a selfie.
inline_images.alt: Person sitting looking out of a window while in a silhouette of two people taking a selfie.

author: Jason Parham
article_content:
As generational cohorts go, Gen Z has been saddled with its share of labels. They scarcely have sex, are “quiet quitters” when it comes to office jobs, and, as they avoid traditional partnership, have learned to solomaxx.

Whether these labels are deserved or completely off the mark, what continually connects this unique class of young people is a desire to reconstruct how they think about connection.

In “Friendship in an Online-Offline World: Digital Life, Connection and Wellbeing” researchers from public polling firm Gallup and the Digital Wellness Lab at Boston Children’s Hospital found that more than one-third of Gen Z (33 percent) rely on AI for companionship. The percentage was higher among daily AI users, spiking to 50 percent, and 42 percent among those with online-only friends.

Rather than measure the consequences of screen time alone, the report examines who Gen Z connects with and how those relationships not only account for their social lives but also how they impact their mental health. While in-person friendships were rated the highest for “strength and support” and were “associated with the most positive emotional experiences,” young people who rely on online-only friends or AI as a social companion may have higher odds of loneliness than those who do not.

Researchers examined three modes of what they consider close connection: in-person friendships, friendships that started IRL but are sustained online, and online-only friendships where a young person has never met their friend in real life. The survey, conducted between May and August, sampled 15,925 people aged 15 to 22 across 16 countries, and suggests that Gen Z benefits more from IRL relationships compared to digital ones, despite nearly half of young people in the US having at least one close online-only friend.

“Adolescence is a time when you thrive when you socialize, and so they’re looking for all of these contexts to socialize in,” says David Bickham, research director of the Digital Wellness Lab. “I don’t necessarily see it as, oh, these kids have some sort of major deficit and are looking to AI. I see it as these are young people who are growing up in a time of AI, the most powerful way to find information online, and the more they use it, they see and are more engaged with the social side of it.”

While AI may help fill a genuine social gap, it hasn’t yet taken the place of their IRL bonds. “In-person and digitally mediated friendships coexist within the same social life,” write the authors of the report.

When it comes to maintaining those affiliations, Instagram and Discord—surprisingly, not TikTok—were the top platforms in the US for staying in touch with online-only friends. Bickham also noted that “loneliness specifically may be something that these online relationships can’t quite compensate for.”

“Kids who are reporting loneliness really do things online that are consistent with trying to make friends. They talk to people they don't know, which is always a risk, but it’s also how you make friends,” Bickham says. The report found that Gen Z men, who were more likely to have digital friendships than women, often encountered new acquaintances through gaming, while young women mentioned social media as their most common category to cultivate connection. “What’s intriguing is that boys who are higher in social anxiety are less likely to make connections. They tend to do things by themselves, but when it comes to AI, what we found is that kids who are still lonely are going to seek out connections” with chatbots, Bickham says.

Recent debates over teen screen time have centered on whether digital devices are driving a youth mental health crisis or if the concerns are overstated. Some critics believe that by only measuring screen time it overlooks the type of content young people watch. This year, social media bans and age-restriction policies for minors took effect in Australia and the UK. In the US, where state legislators have introduced bills to curb addictive design features, a majority of Americans support banning kids under 16 from using social media, according to a recent Pew Research survey.

Jon-Patrick Allem, an associate professor at the Rutgers School of Public Health, wrote last year in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine that research on the topic has primarily focused on “blunt measures of screen time” and that doing so would “treat all content consumed online as uniform.” Allem concluded that this approach is “deficient” and called on researchers to set a new agenda that instead investigates the actual content kids were consuming, not just time spent.

It was also important to Bickham and his team to look beyond a surface-level analysis of screen time and consider the nature of the relationships being formed while young people were online, zeroing in on how that time is spent and who it’s spent with.

“It’s very difficult to measure screen time accurately in a survey. Mainly because half the kids told us this was something they’re doing all the time. A more important finding is the quality of relationship. It’s how you use these platforms that’s going to dictate your outcome, not just how long you use them for.”

A previous report from the Digital Wellness Lab mapped the use of AI among teenagers in the US, Brazil, and France and found that teens aged 13 to 17 were turning to AI for personal advice and creative work, in addition to companionship.

While researchers are wary of classifying the report as a permanent shift in how young people form relationships, they say it does signal a growing reliance on AI companionship as part of a pattern of digital social engagement unfolding among Gen Z.

“It wouldn’t be surprising if AI companionship becomes more common over the next five years as AI becomes integrated into young people’s everyday lives,” says Andrew Dugan, a principal researcher at Gallup. “But whether young people are turning to AI because they feel lonely, or whether AI companionship might reinforce those feelings, remains an important question for future research.”

article_content_zh:
随着一代人的发展，Z 世代已经背负着自己的标签。他们几乎没有性生活，在办公室工作中是“安静的放弃者”，并且由于他们避免传统的伙伴关系，所以学会了独奏。

无论这些标签是实至名归还是完全不合时宜，将这一独特的年轻人阶层不断联系在一起的是重建他们对联系的看法的愿望。

公共民意调查公司盖洛普和波士顿儿童医院数字健康实验室的研究人员在《线上线下世界中的友谊：数字生活、联系和幸福》中发现，超过三分之一的 Z 世代 (33%) 依靠人工智能来陪伴。日常 AI 用户中这一比例更高，飙升至 50%，而那些只在网上交朋友的用户中这一比例为 42%。

该报告并没有单独衡量屏幕时间的影响，而是研究了 Z 世代与谁有联系，以及这些关系如何影响他们的社交生活，以及如何影响他们的心理健康。虽然面对面的友谊在“力量和支持”方面被评为最高，并且“与最积极的情感体验相关”，但依赖网上朋友或人工智能作为社交伴侣的年轻人可能比那些不依赖网络朋友或人工智能的年轻人更容易感到孤独。

研究人员研究了他们认为的密切联系的三种模式：面对面的友谊、在现实生活中开始但在网上维持的友谊，以及年轻人在现实生活中从未见过朋友的纯网络友谊。这项调查于 5 月至 8 月期间进行，对 16 个国家 15,925 名 15 至 22 岁的人进行了抽样调查，结果表明，尽管近一半的美国年轻人至少拥有一位只在网上的亲密朋友，但与数字关系相比，Z 世代从现实关系中受益更多。

数字健康实验室研究主任戴维·比克汉姆 (David Bickham) 表示：“青春期是一个社交能力强的时期，因此他们会寻找所有这些社交环境。” “我不一定认为，哦，这些孩子有某种重大缺陷，正在寻求人工智能。我认为这些年轻人是在人工智能时代长大的，人工智能是在线查找信息的最强大方式，他们使用它的次数越多，他们就会看到并更多地参与其中的社交方面。”

虽然人工智能可能有助于填补真正的社会差距，但它尚未取代他们的现实生活纽带。该报告的作者写道：“面对面的友谊和数字化的友谊在同一个社交生活中共存。”

在维持这些联系方面，Instagram 和 Discord（令人惊讶的是，而不是 TikTok）是美国与只在网上的朋友保持联系的顶级平台。比克汉姆还指出，“特别是孤独感可能是这些在线关系无法完全弥补的。”

“那些表示孤独的孩子确实会在网上做一些与试图交朋友相一致的事情。他们与不认识的人交谈，这总是存在风险，但这也是交朋友的方式，”比克汉姆说。报告发现，Z 世代男性比女性更有可能拥有数字友谊，他们经常通过游戏结识新朋友，而年轻女性则将社交媒体视为最常见的培养联系的类别。 “有趣的是，社交焦虑程度较高的男孩不太可能建立联系。他们倾向于自己做事，但当谈到人工智能时，我们发现仍然孤独的孩子会寻求与聊天机器人的联系”，比克汉姆说。

最近关于青少年屏幕时间的争论集中在数字设备是否正在引发青少年心理健康危机，或者这种担忧是否被夸大了。一些批评者认为，仅衡量屏幕时间会忽略年轻人观看的内容类型。今年，针对未成年人的社交媒体禁令和年龄限制政策在澳大利亚和英国生效。在美国，各州立法者提出了遏制令人上瘾的设计功能的法案，根据皮尤研究中心 (Pew Research) 最近的一项调查，大多数美国人支持禁止 16 岁以下的儿童使用社交媒体。

罗格斯大学公共卫生学院副教授乔恩·帕特里克·阿勒姆（Jon-Patrick Allem）去年在《美国预防医学杂志》上撰文称，该主题的研究主要集中在“对屏幕时间的直接测量”，这样做将“将所有在线消费的内容视为统一的”。阿勒姆得出的结论是，这种方法是“有缺陷的”，并呼吁研究人员制定一个新的议程，调查孩子们实际消费的内容，而不仅仅是花费的时间。

对于比克汉姆和他的团队来说，同样重要的是要超越对屏幕时间的表面分析，并考虑年轻人上网时形成的关系的性质，重点关注如何度过这些时间以及与谁一起度过。

“在调查中准确测量屏幕时间非常困难。主要是因为一半的孩子告诉我们这是他们一直在做的事情。更重要的发现是关系的质量。决定你结果的是你使用这些平台的方式，而不仅仅是你使用它们的时间。”

数字健康实验室之前的一份报告绘制了美国、巴西和法国青少年对人工智能的使用情况，发现 13 至 17 岁的青少年除了寻求陪伴之外，还向人工智能寻求个人建议和创造性工作。

title: YouTube found a new way to inflate view counts
title_en: YouTube found a new way to inflate view counts
author: Emma Roth
article_content:
YouTube’s view counts will now include the number of people that it estimates are watching a video together on TV. In an update on Monday, the platform says it’s bringing “co-views” to public view counts across long-form videos, Shorts, and live content to provide a more “complete picture” of how people are using its platform.

YouTube, which has become even more popular on TVs than phones, also says the change will help it align with “TV industry standards,” which similarly record views by estimating the number of people watching shows. The company says it doesn’t use devices, like cameras or microphones, to estimate how many people are watching a video on TV. Instead, it estimates co-views using a “privacy safe statistical model” that takes into account “demographic patterns and viewing times.”

This marks yet another update to YouTube’s view count system. In August, the platform began counting a view as soon as a video starts playing. The company said at the time that creators will notice their view counts increasing faster as a result of this change, and it seems like adding co-views could boost these numbers as well.

YouTube notes that it will only apply co-views to new views on TV going forward, and that they won’t appear retroactively. Co-views also won’t affect a creator’s ad revenue, YouTube Partner Program eligibility, or revenue.

article_content_zh:
YouTube 的观看次数现在将包括估计在电视上一起观看视频的人数。该平台在周一的更新中表示，它将在长视频、短视频和直播内容的公众观看次数中引入“共同观看次数”，以提供人们如何使用其平台的更“完整的画面”。

YouTube 在电视上比手机上更受欢迎，该公司还表示，这一变化将有助于其与“电视行业标准”保持一致，该标准同样通过估计观看节目的人数来记录观看次数。该公司表示，它不使用摄像头或麦克风等设备来估计有多少人正在观看电视上的视频。相反，它使用“隐私安全统计模型”来估计共同观看次数，该模型考虑了“人口统计模式和观看时间”。

这标志着 YouTube 观看次数系统的又一次更新。八月份，该平台开始在视频开始播放后计算观看次数。该公司当时表示，创作者会注意到，由于这一变化，他们的观看次数增加得更快，而且增加共同观看次数似乎也可以提高这些数字。

YouTube 指出，它只会将共同观看次数应用于未来电视上的新观看次数，并且不会追溯显示。共同观看也不会影响创作者的广告收入、YouTube 合作伙伴计划资格或收入。
