author: Sui-Lee Wee, Aie Balagtas See, and Jes Aznar
article_content:
In May, Roseller Rodriguez, a mayor in the Philippines, was startled to learn from news reports that American officials had arrived in his district to start an artificial intelligence hub.

He saw a video of senior American and Filipino officials standing on a makeshift stage, unveiling a new initiative called Pax Silica.

Mr. Rodriguez had not been invited. Nor had he ever heard about the hub. Was it a data center? Where would the water and electricity come from? What would happen to the farmers living there?

Months later, he says he has few answers.

“I’m not concerned with the geopolitics of Pax Silica,” Mr. Rodriguez said in his office in the municipality of Capas. “My problem is Pax Silica will be built in our community.”

Last December, the United States started Pax Silica to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. The initiative is part of President Trump’s effort to counter Beijing’s economic and technological influence.

Trump administration officials have cast it as a 21st-century successor to “Pax Americana,” the era of relative peace among major powers after World War II.

The significance of Pax Silica, which 26 signatories have joined, has become heightened after revelations that Nvidia’s former chief executive, Jensen Huang, was targeted by Chinese intelligence, exposing the growing geopolitical stakes of the global A.I. race.

In the Philippines, America’s oldest ally in Asia, the backlash has been fierce.

More than 70 organizations formed the Network Opposed to Pax Silica. Farmers, students and activists warn it could drain scarce water and electricity supplies and displace hundreds of Indigenous Ayta people. They plan a demonstration when Mr. Trump is expected to arrive in Manila this week for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

Beyond fears about A.I., the opposition reflects the Philippines’ complicated relationship with its former colonial ruler. Many Filipinos feel a strong cultural affinity for America. But resentment over exploitation runs deep, as does unease over their government’s increasingly close embrace of Washington.

In February, the Philippines signed a memorandum of understanding giving the United States a “first look” at its critical minerals.

“That is unheard-of in the history of our country,” said Renato Reyes Jr., president of Bayan, a political group opposing foreign intervention.

Two months later, the Philippines announced that it had joined Pax Silica and would build a hub about the size of 3,000 football fields. In July, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. pledged that the project would “bring quality jobs to our people, accelerate our industrial competitiveness, and revitalize our economy.”

Local officials wanted to know at what cost.

In August, Roberto Mallari, the Catholic bishop of Tarlac Province, where the hub is planned, met with Joshua Bingcang, head of the government agency overseeing the project. Mr. Rodriguez and other officials were also there.

They pressed Mr. Bingcang on where its power would come from and how many people would be affected.

Mr. Bingcang said the government was considering rainwater harvesting, a desalination plant and a solar farm. More than 100 farmers could be displaced “in the first phase,” he said. Activists estimate the number could be higher.

Bishop Mallari left unconvinced.

“I started to talk about it in my homilies,” he said. “I was telling the parishioners we should get involved in this because we would be the first to be affected.”

Critics question the hub’s resource demands, who would control it and even what it will be.

Government estimates suggest that the project would require up to 90 million liters of water a day and 3 gigawatts of power. Its water needs would require amounts triple the area’s available supply during the dry season, while its projected power demand would be the equivalent of roughly a fifth of Philippine electricity consumption in 2024.

The estimates have fueled suspicions that a sprawling data center is planned. Philippine officials deny this, calling it a semiconductor manufacturing hub.

The State Department was less definite. A spokesman said whether the project would include data centers “will depend on a number of factors, including environmental and infrastructure studies still to come.”

Mr. Bingcang said the project could generate around $3 billion in annual revenue and create up to 190,000 jobs. More than 50 companies, including the world’s tech titans, had expressed interest, he added.

Senator Erwin Tulfo, a politician from a prominent political family, has demanded more clarity on how the hub would operate and whom it would affect, though he remains enthusiastic about the potential jobs.

“It’s money for the country,” he said.

For Senator Imee Marcos, the president’s sister, the issue is sovereignty.

She provided a draft framework that she said was proposed by the Americans. Under its terms, a private “master tenant” would receive a 99-year lease, while a so-called Pax Silica Court in New York would settle disputes.

Ms. Marcos, a critic of her brother’s closer ties to Washington, said she had no objection to an American-led hub.

“You know that the Filipinos love Americans,” she said. “It’s unrequited love, but yeah, it’s unconditional.”

But she warned that the proposed framework could violate Philippine law and the nation’s Constitution, concerns she raised in the Senate.

The State Department denied this, noting that “the Philippines is not transferring land, territory, or sovereign authority to the United States.”

Giovanni Tapang, a former dean of the College of Science at the University of the Philippines Diliman, said supplying the hub’s water needs could require building dams or diverting rivers, depriving farmers of irrigation.

“If we are going to subordinate the development of the country for the U.S.’s needs, then we’re just replicating all the decades of subservience and neocolonial development,” he said.

The proposed Pax Silica site is about a two-hour drive from Manila, in the New Clark City economic zone.

Near a vast stretch of farmland, a sign announcing the project had been taken down. Water buffaloes roam the area. Just 12 miles away stands the former Clark Air Base, once one of America’s largest overseas military bases.

For the Indigenous Ayta people who live nearby, the threat of displacement is painfully familiar.

About 200 Ayta families live in Manabayucan, a remote village on the edge of the planned hub. The Aytas, among the Philippines’ earliest inhabitants, are also among its poorest.

Many were displaced during the Philippine-American War at the turn of the 20th century as the United States established a fort that became the precursor to Clark Air Base.

After Mount Pinatubo, a nearby volcano, erupted in 1991, many people spent years in government camps, unable to resume farming. That same year, the Philippines forced the Americans out of their military bases. But the land was never returned to the Aytas. It passed to the Philippine government.

Reaching Manabayucan requires a drive along an unpaved road, a river crossing and a hike up a steep hill. The village has no electricity, running water or mobile phone coverage.

The outside world feels far away, but now it is closing in.

Nearby, a bulldozer had dug up an Ayta cemetery in what residents said was the beginning of the Pax Silica project.

Many villagers have never heard of artificial intelligence. They know nothing of the fierce opposition to data centers in the United States.

But they understand what losing their land would mean.

Roby Dalis, an Ayta farmer who cannot read or write, earns $4.70 a day selling banana leaves. He recently joined his first protest, traveling to Manila to march alongside other farmers.

“If they take the land where we live, we will have nowhere to go,” Mr. Dalis said.

The Aytas’ plight has become a rallying cause for the movement against Pax Silica. On a recent Thursday, villagers gathered outside their bamboo huts to hear from Kim Falyao, a youth Indigenous activist.

“We should not be dictated upon by anyone saying, ‘We want to build Pax Silica here, so move out,’" she said, as villagers nodded. “No. We have the right to decide for ourselves and our community.”

A day earlier, an Ayta farmer, Nelson de Guzman, spoke at a protest near the presidential palace in Manila. Students held signs reading: “No to Pax Silica.” Protesters destroyed a painted likeness of Mr. Trump.

Mr. de Guzman stepped up to the microphone.

“We need our land,” he said. “We don’t need Pax Silica, and most importantly, we don’t need the U.S.”

The crowd erupted in cheers.

summary_en: The U.S.-led AI hub initiative in the Philippines faces local opposition due to concerns over forced displacement, strained water and electricity resources, and potential erosion of digital sovereignty. This incident underscores the socio-political friction inherent in U.S. efforts to project technological infrastructure into the Indo-Pacific region.
title_zh: 特朗普的人工智能计划霸权助长菲律宾的抵抗
summary_zh: 美国主导的菲律宾AI枢纽建设引发当地社区强烈抵制，主要围绕土地征用、公共资源消耗及国家主权风险展开
article_content_zh:
今年 5 月，菲律宾市长罗塞尔·罗德里格斯 (Roseller Rodriguez) 从新闻报道中惊讶地获悉，美国官员已抵达他所在的地区，启动人工智能中心。

他看到一段视频，美国和菲律宾高级官员站在临时舞台上，推出了一项名为“Pax Silica”的新举措。

罗德里格斯先生没有受到邀请。他也从未听说过这个枢纽。这是一个数据中心吗？水和电从哪里来？住在那里的农民会怎样？

几个月后，他说他几乎没有答案。

“我不关心 Pax Silica 的地缘政治，”罗德里格斯在卡帕斯市的办公室里说。 “我的问题是 Pax Silica 将建在我们的社区中。”

去年 12 月，美国启动了 Pax Silica，旨在联合人工智能领域的合作伙伴。供应链独立于中国。该倡议是特朗普总统对抗北京经济和技术影响力的努力的一部分。

特朗普政府官员将其视为“美国和平”的21世纪继承者，“美国和平”是二战后大国之间相对和平的时代。

在英伟达前首席执行官黄仁勋成为中国情报部门目标的消息曝光后，已有 26 名签署者加入的 Pax Silica 的重要性变得更加突出，暴露了全球人工智能日益增长的地缘政治利益。种族。

美国在亚洲最古老的盟友菲律宾对此的强烈反对。

70 多个组织组成了反对 Pax Silica 网络。农民、学生和活动人士警告说，这可能会耗尽稀缺的水和电力供应，并使数百名艾塔原住民流离失所。他们计划在特朗普预计本周抵达马尼拉参加东南亚国家联盟峰会时举行示威活动。

除了对人工智能的担忧之外，反对派还反映出菲律宾与其前殖民统治者的复杂关系。许多菲律宾人对美国有很强的文化亲和力。但对剥削的不满情绪根深蒂固，对政府日益亲近华盛顿的不安也是如此。

今年二月，菲律宾签署了一份谅解备忘录，让美国“优先了解”其关键矿产。

“这在我们国家的历史上是闻所未闻的，”反对外国干预的政治组织“Bayan”的主席小雷纳托·雷耶斯(Renato Reyes Jr.)说。

两个月后，菲律宾宣布加入Pax Silica，并将建设一个约3000个足球场大小的枢纽。 7月，总统小费迪南德·R·马科斯承诺该项目将“为我们的人民带来优质就业机会，提高我们的工业竞争力，并振兴我们的经济。”

当地官员想知道代价是多少。

8月，规划该中心的打拉省天主教主教罗伯托·马拉里(Roberto Mallari)会见了负责监督该项目的政府机构负责人约书亚·宾仓(Joshua Bingcang)。罗德里格斯先生和其他官员也在场。

他们向冰仓先生追问，其权力从何而来，有多少人会受到影响。

丙仓表示，政府正在考虑雨水收集、海水淡化厂和太阳能发电厂。他说，“第一阶段”可能有 100 多名农民流离失所。活动人士估计这个数字可能会更高。

马拉里主教不服气地离开了。

“我开始在讲道中谈论这个问题，”他说。 “我告诉教区居民我们应该参与其中，因为我们将是第一个受到影响的人。”

批评者质疑该中心的资源需求、谁将控制它，甚至它会是什么。

政府估计该项目每天需要多达 9000 万升水和 3 吉瓦电力。其用水需求将是该地区旱季可用供应量的三倍，而预计电力需求将相当于 2024 年菲律宾用电量的约五分之一。

这些估计引发了人们对正在规划建设一个庞大数据中心的怀疑。菲律宾官员否认这一点，称其为半导体制造中心。

国务院的说法不太明确。一位发言人表示，该项目是否包括数据中心“将取决于许多因素，包括仍有待进行的环境和基础设施研究。”

丙仓表示，该项目每年可产生约30亿美元收入，并创造多达19万个就业岗位。他补充说，包括全球科技巨头在内的 50 多家公司表示了兴趣。

来自著名政治世家的参议员欧文·塔尔福 (Erwin Tulfo) 要求更明确地说明该中心将如何运作以及它将影响谁，但他仍然对潜在的就业机会充满热情。

“这是国家的钱，”他说。

对于总统的妹妹、参议员伊米·马科斯来说，问题在于主权。

她提供了一个框架草案，她说这是美国人提出的。根据其条款，私人“主租户”将获得 99 年的租约，而纽约所谓的 Pax Silica 法院将解决纠纷。

马科斯女士批评她哥哥与华盛顿关系更密切，她表示，她不反对建立一个由美国主导的中心。

“你知道菲律宾人热爱美国人，”她说。 “这是单相思，但是，是的，这是无条件的。”

但她警告说，拟议的框架可能违反菲律宾法律和国家宪法，这是她在参议院提出的担忧。

美国国务院否认了这一点，并指出“菲律宾没有向美国转让土地、领土或主权。”

菲律宾迪利曼大学理学院前院长乔瓦尼·塔庞表示，满足该中心的用水需求可能需要修建水坝或改道河流，从而导致农民无法进行灌溉。

他说：“如果我们要让国家的发展服从于美国的需要，那么我们只是在重复几十年来的屈从和新殖民主义发展。”

拟建的 Pax Silica 工厂位于新克拉克市经济区，距马尼拉约两小时车程。

在一大片农田附近，宣布该项目的标志已被拆除。水牛在该地区漫步。距离酒店仅 12 英里的是前克拉克空军基地，这里曾经是美国最大的海外军事基地之一。

对于居住在附近的艾塔原住民来说，流离失所的威胁是非常熟悉的。

大约 200 个艾塔家庭居住在马纳巴尤坎 (Manabayucan)，这是规划枢纽边缘的一个偏远村庄。艾塔人是菲律宾最早的居民，也是最贫穷的人之一。

二十世纪之交的美菲战争期间，美国建立了一座堡垒，后来成为克拉克空军基地的前身，许多人流离失所。

1991 年附近的皮纳图博火山喷发后，许多人在政府营地里度过了数年，无法恢复耕种。同年，菲律宾迫使美国人离开其军事基地。但这片土地从未归还给艾塔人。它已转交给菲律宾政府。

到达马纳巴尤坎需要沿着一条未铺砌的道路行驶，穿越河流并徒步爬上一座陡峭的山坡。该村没有电、自来水或移动电话覆盖。

外面的世界感觉很遥远，但现在却很近。

附近，一台推土机挖出了艾塔墓地，居民称这是 Pax Silica 项目的开始。

许多村民从未听说过人工智能。他们对美国对数据中心的强烈反对一无所知。

但他们明白失去土地意味着什么。

罗比·达利斯 (Roby Dalis) 是一位不会读写的艾塔农民，靠卖香蕉叶每天赚取 4.70 美元。他最近参加了他的第一次抗议活动，前往马尼拉与其他农民一起游行。

“如果他们夺走了我们居住的土地，我们将无处可去，”达利斯先生说。

艾塔人的困境已成为反对“和平硅”运动的一个集结理由。最近的一个星期四，村民们聚集在竹屋外，聆听青年土著活动家 Kim Falyao 的讲话。

“我们不应该听从任何人的指令，‘我们想在这里建造 Pax Silica，所以搬出去’”，她说道，村民们纷纷点头。 “不。我们有权为自己和社区做出决定。”

一天前，艾塔农民纳尔逊·德古兹曼在马尼拉总统府附近的抗议活动中发表讲话。学生们举着牌子，上面写着：“对 Pax Silica 说不。”抗议者毁坏了特朗普的肖像画。

德古兹曼先生走到麦克风前。

“我们需要我们的土地，”他说。 “我们不需要 Pax Silica，最重要的是，我们不需要美国。”

title: Biggest IPOs this year lose investors money as AI frenzy fades
title_en: Biggest IPOs this year lose investors money as AI frenzy fades
author: Emily Herbert
article_content:
The biggest IPOs in history have raised tens of billions of dollars each, and delivered returns ranging from significant gains to sustained losses.

Saudi Aramco raised $25.6 billion in its December 2019 initial public offering, setting the record for the largest in history. SpaceX (SPCX -0.59%) raised $75 billion on June 12, 2026, offering 555.6 million shares at $135 each, nearly three times the record set by Saudi Aramco. Shares closed their first day of trading up 19% at $160.95, giving the company a market capitalization of roughly $2.1 trillion.

SpaceX may not hold the record for the biggest IPO for long, however. On June 1, Anthropic confidentially filed paperwork for an IPO and reportedly aims to match or exceed SpaceX's raise, which climbed to $86.2 billion once its overallotment option was exercised, on top of the $75 billion raised at the outset. Separately, investors are reportedly targeting a valuation of $2 trillion or more.

At that valuation, Anthropic's IPO would value the company higher than SpaceX's IPO did. And if Anthropic's IPO proceeds match or exceed SpaceX's $86.2 billion total, it would set the record for capital raised as well. Anthropic has not set a share price, count, or confirmed valuation target.

Here's how the 10 biggest IPOs currently stack up against each other.

The 10 biggest offerings on record offer a useful frame of reference for investors. Together, they raised more than $180 billion.

Their returns tell very different stories.

The two best long-run performers in the top 10 had opposite first-year experiences.

Visa (V +1.30%) went public in March 2008 at a split-adjusted offer price of $11, during the global financial crisis. It gained 92% in its first three months and has returned 2,854% from that offer price as of May 2026, according to FactSet data. Visa earns fees on payment processing volume and does not extend credit, which insulated it from the default risk that defined the 2008 crisis.

Meta Platforms (META +2.90%) (formerly Facebook) had the worst first three months of any company in the top 10, falling 47% from its May 2012 IPO price of $38. Investors who bought on day one lost roughly a third of their money in the first year. By year five the stock was up 289%. Total return since the 2012 offer price: +1,572% as of May 2026, according to FactSet data.

AIA Group (SEHK:1299) and ICBC (IDCBF -3.85%), both listed in Hong Kong, delivered steadier compounding with less short-term volatility than the technology companies. AIA returned 318% since its 2010 IPO; ICBC's H-Share returned 116% since 2006.

Three of the 10 largest IPOs were negative at the 5-year mark, and a fourth spent most of its first five years below its offer price. In each case, the company was influenced by sector dynamics.

Saudi Aramco is down 13% since its December 2019 offer price, the worst total return in the group, according to investing.com data. The company listed at the end of a decade in which energy's share of global equity indexes declined, and oil prices have not consistently supported the valuation implied at the IPO price.

SoftBank Corp (SFBQF -3.19%), the Japanese telecom subsidiary, not SoftBank Group, fell 15% on its first day of trading in December 2018, according to FactSet data, and spent most of the following five years below its offer price. Total return from the split-adjusted offer price of 150 JPY: +43% as of May 2026, according to FactSet data. A mature telecommunications business with limited growth levers attracted limited long-term capital.

NTT DoCoMo gained 47% in its first year after its October 1998 IPO, then fell sharply with the broader telecom sector. By year three, it was down 48% from the IPO price. NTT took the company private in 2020.

Enel SpA (ENL -1.61%) raised $16.5 billion in its 1999 Italian privatization. Total return in euros from the split-adjusted offer price of €7.31: +31% as of May 2026, according to FactSet data.

The five companies with the highest total returns, Visa, Meta, AIA Group, ICBC, and General Motors, are all financials, technology, or consumer companies. The four weakest performers span energy, telecom, and utilities.

The performance table in the introduction shows returns over five periods of time from IPO.

In the first three months, five of the 10 biggest IPOs had negative returns. Meta fell 47%. Saudi Aramco fell 23%. NTT DoCoMo and SoftBank Corp both fell roughly 10%, and Enel SpA fell 3%. Of the five that gained, Visa (+92%) and ICBC (+48%) posted the largest jumps. Both are financial companies, not tech stocks, so they weren't exposed to the tech-sector swings that hit Meta.

At the one-year mark, the picture is mixed. Five of the 10 were still negative one year in. NTT DoCoMo was the outlier at +47%, benefiting from late-1990s telecom enthusiasm before the sector reversed. Visa and ICBC were positive. Meta and General Motors were both down more than 30%.

At the five-year mark, the split between sector winners and losers becomes clear. The financials and technology companies had largely recovered and compounded their gains. The energy, telecom, and utilities names had not. Enel was down 16% at five years; NTT DoCoMo was down 48%; Saudi Aramco was down 11%.

Total return since IPO reinforces the sector gap. The difference between the best (Visa, +2,854%) and the worst (Aramco, -13%) is not primarily a reflection of how much each company raised. It is driven by sector, timing, and business model durability over the full period.

"On average, IPOs, particularly larger ones, disappoint investors during their first year," said Lou Whiteman, contributing Motley Fool stock analyst. "Larger IPOs tend to attract a lot of hype, and as the excitement fades, so too does buying interest."

Insider lockup expirations can compound that effect by increasing the supply of shares as the first year progresses. By year five, Whiteman said, those temporary factors fade and the stock trades more on fundamentals, though if the original valuation was stretched, "the fundamentals might not support an elevated stock price."

His advice for investors: stay patient amid initial post-IPO volatility, and make a fresh assessment after the market has adjusted to the company regularly reporting earnings.

Two patterns may be relevant for investors evaluating SpaceX months after its record-shattering IPO, and preparing for Anthropic's highly anticipated stock market debut.

First, IPO size doesn't meaningfully impact long-term performance. Saudi Aramco, the largest IPO outside of SpaceX, had the worst long-term performance, while the best performing, Visa, raised roughly $8 billion less than Saudi Aramco. Among the 10 biggest IPOs, the five with the best long-term performance had deal sizes between $14 billion and $17.9 billion.

Second, sector has some bearing on performance. IPOs in financials, technology, and consumer discretionary have had strong long-term performances while energy, telecom, or utilities have posted weaker returns. SpaceX spans multiple categories, which makes it difficult for investors to judge based on history. That's not the only surprise it's shown since debuting, and some early, new lessons could apply to Anthropic's expected IPO later this year.

"Anthropic’s size makes it unique in history, but we do have one prominent recent example to compare it to: SpaceX," Whiteman said. "The interesting thing about SpaceX’s trading so far is that all of the things we thought would move the stock – adding it to the indexes, lockup releases – have not moved the stock as expected."

He attributed that to how widely anticipated those events were, allowing traders to price them in. "I would suspect Anthropic would follow a similar trajectory, which makes stock movements hard to predict."

That points back to Whiteman's original advice for investors: stay patient, even amid the hype of mega-IPOs.

"IPOs are exciting, and the companies behind the offerings can be great long-term investments," Whiteman said. "But waiting out the initial volatility and allowing some of the dust to settle from lockup expirations and the company adjusting to the regular reporting cadence of being public allows for a more sober assessment of the business and a price that better reflects its strengths and limitations."

Jack Caporal is the Research Director for The Motley Fool and Motley Fool Money. Jack leads efforts to identify and analyze trends shaping investing and personal financial decisions across the United States. His research has appeared in thousands of media outlets including Harvard Business Review, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and CNBC, and has been cited in congressional testimony. He previously covered business and economic trends as a reporter and policy analyst in Washington, D.C. He serves as Chair of the Trade Policy Committee at the World Trade Center in Denver, Colorado. He holds a B.A. degree in International Relations with a concentration in International Economics from Michigan State University.

Jack Caporal has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Meta Platforms and Visa. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

title_zh: 随着人工智能热潮的消退，今年最大的首次公开募股（IPO）让投资者损失了资金
summary_zh: 2026年十大IPO表现逊色，较发行价平均下跌20.5%，反映出市场对AI热潮引发的过高溢价回归理性
article_content_zh:
历史上规模最大的首次公开募股每次都筹集了数百亿美元，并带来了从显着收益到持续亏损的回报。

沙特阿美公司在 2019 年 12 月的首次公开募股中筹集了 256 亿美元，创下了历史上最大的IPO 纪录。 SpaceX (SPCX -0.59%) 于 2026 年 6 月 12 日筹集了 750 亿美元，以每股 135 美元的价格发行了 5.556 亿股股票，几乎是沙特阿美公司创下的纪录的三倍。首日交易收盘，该公司股价上涨 19%，至 160.95 美元，市值约为 2.1 万亿美元。

然而，SpaceX 的最大 IPO 记录可能不会保持太久。 6 月 1 日，Anthropic 秘密提交了首次公开募股 (IPO) 的文件，据报道，其目标是追平或超过 SpaceX 的融资规模。在行使超额配股权后，该公司在最初筹集的 750 亿美元基础上攀升至 862 亿美元。另外，据报道投资者的目标估值为 2 万亿美元或更高。

按照这个估值，Anthropic 的 IPO 对该公司的估值将高于 SpaceX 的 IPO。如果 Anthropic 的 IPO 募集资金等于或超过 SpaceX 的 862 亿美元总额，也将创下筹集资金的记录。 Anthropic 尚未设定股价、数量或确认的估值目标。

以下是目前 10 家最大的 IPO 的比较。

有记录以来最大的 10 次发行为投资者提供了有用的参考框架。他们总共筹集了超过 1800 亿美元。

他们的回报讲述了截然不同的故事。

前十名中长期表现最好的两名球员在第一年的经历却截然相反。

Visa (V +1.30%) 于 2008 年 3 月在全球金融危机期间以分割调整后的发行价 11 美元上市。根据 FactSet 的数据，该公司在前三个月上涨了 92%，截至 2026 年 5 月，其回报率较发行价上涨了 2,854%。 Visa 根据支付处理量收取费用，并且不提供信贷，这使其免受 2008 年危机的违约风险的影响。

Meta Platforms (META +2.90%)（前身为 Facebook）是前 10 名公司中前三个月表现最差的，较 2012 年 5 月 38 美元的 IPO 价格下跌了 47%。第一天买入的投资者在第一年损失了大约三分之一的资金。到第五年，该股股价上涨了 289%。根据 FactSet 数据，截至 2026 年 5 月，自 2012 年发行价以来的总回报率为 +1,572%。

与科技公司相比，在香港上市的友邦保险集团（SEHK：1299）和中国工商银行（IDCBF -3.85%）的复利更稳定，短期波动更小。自 2010 年 IPO 以来，友邦保险的回报率为 318%；自2006年以来，工行H股回报率达116%。

十大首次公开募股中，有三宗在五年内出现负值，第四宗在前五年的大部分时间里都低于其发行价。在每种情况下，公司都受到行业动态的影响。

根据Investing.com的数据，沙特阿美公司自2019年12月的报价以来已下跌13%，是该集团中总回报率最差的。该公司上市的十年末，能源在全球股票指数中所占的份额有所下降，而油价也未能始终支撑IPO价格隐含的估值。

FactSet 数据显示，日本电信子公司软银公司 (SFBQF -3.19%) 在 2018 年 12 月的首个交易日下跌 15%，并且在接下来五年的大部分时间里都低于其发行价。根据 FactSet 数据，截至 2026 年 5 月，分割调整后 150 日元发行价的总回报率为 +43%。成熟的电信业务增长杠杆有限，吸引的长期资本有限。

title: Biggest IPOs this year lose investors money as AI frenzy fades
title_en: Biggest IPOs this year lose investors money as AI frenzy fades

Biggest IPOs this year lose investors money as AI frenzy fades

inline_images.alt: A SpaceX billboard outside the Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square on the day of the company’s IPO © Jeenah Moon/Reuters

inline_images.alt: What has been a blockbuster market for bankers is proving a less favourable one for many investors © Michael Nagle/Bloomberg

author: Emily Herbert
article_content:
Shares in Wall Street’s 10 biggest initial public offerings this year have since lost a fifth of their value, fuelling concerns ahead of Anthropic’s blockbuster listing that a blizzard of issuance is hurting equity markets.

The US IPO market has roared back to life this year, with the deal value of listings already at the highest this decade, powered in large part by mega flotations from SpaceX this summer and Claude maker Anthropic this week.

But what has been a windfall for bankers advising on the IPOs is proving less favourable for many investors, as concerns have grown over the sustainability of the AI boom.

FT analysis of the 10 biggest IPOs of the year shows that the companies’ share prices have since fallen by an average of 20.5 per cent from the offer price.

By contrast, in the previous four years, the share prices of the 10 biggest Wall Street IPOs ended the year higher. Even in 2022, when the S&P 500 fell 19.4 per cent, IPO investors would still have made money.

“IPO performance has been awful this year — the class of 2026 has produced very little,” said one senior executive at a large US asset manager. “Asset managers tend to want to protect performance into year-end . . . if [Anthropic] doesn’t go well, it could screw up my entire year.”

The sheer volume of equity coming to the market this year as well as a barrage of new debt issuance by tech giants has weighed on performance, said Sanjay Rijhsinghani, chief investment officer of LGT Wealth Management.

“There is just so much issuance going on in the bond and equity market,” he said. “There is a bit of fatigue.”

Among AI-related IPOs, he added, investor exuberance may have pushed offer prices too high, making it harder for stocks to perform well after listing.

“None of these IPOs are coming at bargain-basement prices,” Rijhsinghani said. “These IPOs are not easy to value — you’re buying a future price which may or may not materialise; that is playing on people’s minds.”

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

John Ettinger, senior portfolio manager at Federated Hermes, said: “There are more big deals down a lot [this year] than I have seen at any point in my career.”

Investor demand remains strong for the biggest names at the point of listing. Anthropic began its investor roadshow last week after filing documents with regulators setting out its plans to sell 825mn shares at a price range of $70-$78, which would value the company at up to $1.4tn.

The FT later reported that the AI giant’s bankers were considering raising the IPO price after receiving heavy demand from investors.

However, appetite has often waned following flotations. The biggest IPO of the year so far, SpaceX, soared at its listing, but within days sank back. It has spent much of the past month trading around the offer price of $135.

Ettinger said the recent slumps in post-IPO share prices have given him reason to think he would rather have some “dry powder” to invest in the secondary market at a lower price “if it’s a name we like”, rather than participating at flotation.

“In this IPO market you have to be a bit discerning . . . and realise if this is an IPO which you might be able to pick up cheaper in a few months.”

The Anthropic listing is coming to the market at a volatile time for the AI trade. Chip stocks sold off sharply during October, as third-quarter earnings season sparked fears among investors that the vast amount of capital being ploughed into AI infrastructure may not translate into a sufficient return on investment.

The sell-off deepened after the US midterm elections in early November. Fears emerged that the Democrats’ sweeping victory — including in states and districts where they campaigned on an anti-data centre platform — would prompt a policy backlash against the AI build-out.

“This is a brutal backdrop to be launching a tech IPO,” said the executive at the large US asset manager, so soon after the brutal chip stocks sell-off after the Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections. Since then, the Nasdaq 100 has recovered most of its losses, but US stocks remain volatile.

While performance is a worry for some investors heading into the end of the year, few seem keen to miss out on the Anthropic listing.

“Anthropic is the first pure-play AI [stock] . . . we haven’t got anything else like that in the market,” Rijhsinghani at LGT said.

Federated Hermes’ Ettinger added: “Good companies that are executing, growing, coming at a reasonable valuation are going to be able to get done in any market.”

article_content_zh:
今年华尔街10大首次公开募股的股票此后已下跌了五分之一，这加剧了人们在Anthropic即将进行轰动性上市之际的担忧，即发行潮正在冲击股市。

今年，美国IPO市场重现活力，上市交易额已达到本十年来的最高水平，这在很大程度上得益于今年夏天SpaceX的巨额上市以及本周Claude的开发商Anthropic的上市。

但对于为这些公司提供咨询服务的银行家来说，这却是一笔意外之财。

美国一家大型资产管理公司的一位高管表示：“今年 IPO 的表现很糟糕——2026 年的IPO 产出很少。” “资产管理公司往往希望将业绩维持到年底……如果 [Anthropic] 进展不顺利，可能会毁了我一整年。”

LGT 财富管理公司首席投资官 Sanjay Rijhsinghani 表示，今年进入市场的大量股票以及科技巨头发行的大量新债券对业绩造成了压力。

“债券和股票市场的发行量如此之大，”他说。 “有一点疲劳。”

他补充说，在人工智能相关的首次公开募股中，投资者的热情可能导致发行价过高，从而使股票在上市后更难表现良好。

Rijhsinghani 表示：“这些首次公开募股都不会以低廉的价格进行。” “这些首次公开募股并不容易估值——你购买的是未来的价格，它可能会实现，也可能不会实现；这正在影响人们的想法。”

Federated Hermes的高级投资组合经理John Ettinger表示：“[今年]大幅缩水的巨额交易比我职业生涯中见过的任何时候都要多。”

在上市之际，投资者对知名大公司的需求依然强劲。Anthropic上周向监管机构提交了文件，阐述其计划以70-78美元的价格区间出售8.25亿股股份，这将使该公司的估值高达1.4万亿美元，随后便开始了投资者路演。

《金融时报》后来报道称，这家人工智能巨头的银行家们……

Anthropic 的上市正值人工智能行业的动荡时期。由于第三季度财报季引发投资者担心投入人工智能基础设施的大量资金可能无法转化为足够的投资回报，芯片股在 10 月份大幅抛售。

11 月初美国中期选举后，抛售进一步加剧。人们担心民主党的压倒性胜利——包括他们在反数据中心平台上竞选的州和地区——将引发针对人工智能建设的政策反弹。

这家美国大型资产管理公司的高管表示，在民主党在美国中期选举中大获全胜后芯片股遭到残酷抛售后不久，这家美国大型资产管理公司的高管表示：“在这样的背景下发起科技股IPO是残酷的。”此后，纳斯达克100指数已收复大部分失地，但美股仍持续波动。

虽然一些投资者在年底前对业绩表现感到担忧，但似乎很少有人愿意错过 Anthropic 的上市。

LGT 的 Rijhsinghani 表示：“Anthropic 是第一只纯人工智能股票……我们在市场上还没有类似的产品。”

Federated Hermes的Ettinger补充道：“正在执行战略、正在成长且估值合理的优秀公司将在任何市场都能取得成功。”

title: Preliminary report: Microsoft attributes a major 365 and Exchange outage to a software defect introduced in a July 2026 update for network gateway servers (Richard Speed/The Register)
title_en: Preliminary report: Microsoft attributes a major 365 and Exchange outage to a software defect introduced in a July 2026 update for network gateway servers (Richard Speed/The Register)

inline_images.caption: Aerial view of a large industrial site with DataVIta
inline_images.alt: Aerial view of a large industrial site with DataVIta

author: The Register
article_content:
Microsoft has blamed last week's epic outage on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email.

According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact.

However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted."

"The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware."

The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued.

It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and… you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive."

So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help – they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again.

"Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old.

Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored.

The timings show the pain customers experienced and the floundering in Redmond as Microsoft tried to work out why Exchange Online and other cloud services were so poorly. The Teams failover, which turned out to be a factor in the outage, happened at 0107 UTC on November 12. During the day, the load began to ramp up until, at 1603 UTC, Microsoft's connectivity anomaly detection monitor identified an increase in connectivity issues.

At 1633 UTC, the first support case came in.

It is not difficult to imagine the stress engineers felt as, over the next 15 hours, nothing they tried resolved the issue. All ongoing and planned deployments and configuration changes were paused while the team attempted to resurrect the service. Extra capacity was added. Traffic was rerouted. Yet servers kept falling over.

"Those services that were able – like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps – failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure," the report says. "But not all services, like Exchange Online, can fail out of this network gateway for scale reasons."

Hence the length of time for which Exchange Online (or, from the perspective of many users, Outlook) was out of action.

By 0030 UTC on November 13, Microsoft had identified connection negotiation as the main culprit for the access failures and concluded that competing processes were preventing connections from being handled.

However, it took until 0720 UTC before "We identified a mitigation and applied the mitigation – an update that reverted the defective change."

At 1610 UTC, Microsoft confirmed that things were once again looking healthy and, at 0415 on November 14, issued its final customer update.

A final post incident report is due on November 20. However, the preliminary report will do little to calm jangling nerves. An update applied three months ago managed to cause Exchange Online (and other services) disruption on a global scale? With load testing that didn't reflect scenarios under Microsoft's control?

The engineers who worked feverishly to restore services deserve commendation and will hopefully never have to buy their own beverages in Redmond again (or at least escape the next round of firings). However, the processes that led to an update with a latent defect reaching production deserve a long, hard look. ®

article_content_zh:
微软将上周的大规模宕机归咎于它在 7 月份所做的一项更改，该更改潜伏在网络网关服务器中，直到负载激增和容量下降触发了该缺陷，从而使 Microsoft 365 世界暂停了一天的电子邮件。

根据微软 11 月 15 日发布的初步事件后报告，该缺陷于 2026 年 7 月引入。微软表示，该更新当时看起来不错，已通过负载测试并部署，没有任何影响。

然而，测试还不够好。微软的报告指出：“我们的负载测试往往侧重于内核较少的较弱硬件。”该缺陷导致“内部 Windows 进程内部发生锁争用，导致机器资源（CPU 和内存）耗尽”。

“在具有更多内核和更新硬件的机器上，争用问题会更加严重。”

包含该缺陷的修复是专门为 Microsoft 365 网络网关服务器准备的。然后两件事同时发生了。团队故障转移到支持 Exchange Online 的“主”网关，导致负载激增，这本身并不特别不寻常。与此同时，网络网关近 14% 的服务器容量停止服务，这本身也不是问题：它正在恢复，并且根据微软的说法，“该服务有足够的容量空间”。他们一起推开了通往缺陷的大门，混乱随之而来。

这是一个典型的级联故障场景。当服务器失去连接时，流量将路由到下一个健康端点。哪位遇到同样的问题。所以交通再次改变路线……你可以看到这是怎么回事。两个小时内，整个 Microsoft 团队都遇到了该缺陷。报告指出，“最低时，超过 80% 的服务器没有响应。”

那么，该怎么办呢？让服务器恢复服务并没有帮助——它们立即不堪重负并再次倒下。

“我们通常的自动恢复流程并不是为了从这种广泛的无响应状态中恢复服务而设计的。”直接回滚也是不可能的，因为缺陷已经存在几个月了。

相反，工程师们为该补丁开发了补丁，或者用微软的话说，“一个更新，将代码路径恢复到 Windows 中之前已知的良好状态”。补丁已应用于多组服务器，服务逐渐恢复。

这些时间安排显示了当微软试图找出 Exchange Online 和其他云服务如此糟糕的原因时，客户所经历的痛苦和雷德蒙德的困境。 Teams 故障转移发生在 11 月 12 日 0107 UTC（世界标准时间 0107 点），这被证明是导致中断的一个因素。白天，负载开始增加，直到 1603 UTC（世界标准时间），Microsoft 连接异常检测监视器发现连接问题有所增加。

世界标准时间 1633 年，第一个支持案例出现。

不难想象，在接下来的 15 个小时里，工程师们所感受到的压力是他们尝试过的任何方法都无法解决问题。当团队尝试恢复服务时，所有正在进行和计划的部署和配置更改都已暂停。增加了额外的容量。交通已改道。然而服务器不断崩溃。

报告称：“那些能够运行的服务，例如 Teams、OneDrive、SharePoint 和 Office 应用程序，由于网络网关基础设施出现故障而失败了。” “但并非所有服务（例如 Exchange Online）都会因规模原因而无法通过此网络网关。”

因此，Exchange Online（或者从许多用户的角度来看，Outlook）无法运行的时间长度。

title: Big Tech Mounts Last-Ditch Push to Rewrite Canada’s Data Access Bill
title_en: Big Tech Mounts Last-Ditch Push to Rewrite Canada’s Data Access Bill
author: Laura Osman
article_content:
Big Tech Mounts Last-Ditch Push to Rewrite Canada’s Data Access Bill Bloomberg · Photographer: Betty Laura Zapata/Bloomberg Laura Osman Mon, 16 November 2026 at 3:00 am GMT-8 5 min read (Bloomberg) -- Prime Minister Mark Carney's government is facing fierce pushback from Big Tech firms over security legislation that would require companies to retain and hand over user data to law enforcement.

Lobbyists and executives from Meta Platforms Inc., Apple Inc. and Alphabet Inc. are mounting a last-ditch blitz in Ottawa to rewrite the bill before it passes. On Monday, leaders from Meta, Signal Messenger LLC and Tailscale Inc. will take their fight to a key Senate committee hearing that will shape the legislation's final form.

Bill C-22, so-called "lawful access" legislation, is designed to allow Canada's spy agency and police services to compel electronic service providers to preserve and turn over certain metadata. The government insists the measures simply align Canada with its Five Eyes and Group of Seven allies.

Tech firms, privacy advocates and US lawmakers counter that the bill goes far beyond frameworks adopted by Canada's peers, warning it would threaten platform security and user privacy. Meta has argued the law would effectively conscript its platforms as "an arm of the government's surveillance apparatus."

"There's a real possibility that both the security and the privacy of Canadian users of these systems is really undermined," Rachel Curran, Meta's head of public policy in Canada, said in an interview.

For Carney's government, the battle risks chilling tech investment, escalating tensions with the US and driving privacy-focused platforms out of the Canadian market. Signal has threatened to pull out of Canada if the bill passes in its current form. Proton AG, a Swiss tech firm, has said it would rethink its expansion plans in the country.

The bill's critics object to a rule that would let the government force electronic service providers to retain certain user metadata for up to six months so it can be disclosed to law enforcement officials, if needed.

The proposed law could also compel some firms to unlock encrypted data — but only if they built the encryption and possess the information necessary to unlock it. Earlier this year, lawmakers amended the bill to make clear that companies also cannot be forced to introduce a "systemic vulnerability" into their software.

Those guardrails were meant to ease fears from firms like Signal and Meta, which owns WhatsApp, that the bill targeted end-to-end encryption. That form of encryption ensures only the sender and receiver can read the messages — meaning the company doesn't have the ability to decrypt them.

Even so, privacy advocates and tech leaders argue that the bill still gives the government sweeping power to order firms to build "technical capabilities" to intercept communications and hand over data.

Tech companies have long warned they cannot create "backdoor" access only for law enforcement without weakening security for all users. Curran said an order that would make Meta's systems more vulnerable is a "red line" for the company, and likely its industry peers as well.

"It probably puts Canada in a position where there's going to eventually be a bit of a standoff between service providers and the government, and it's not good for Canadians," she said.

The UK and Apple faced a similar dispute last year when the government ordered the company to circumvent encryption that the company uses to secure user data stored on its cloud services. Apple challenged the order and removed its advanced data protection feature for British users. The case is still before the courts.

"In the hypothetical future, if we faced similar orders, we would have to consider those options," Curran said.

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree has said the bill has already been amended to alleviate the concerns raised by Apple in the UK about the potential impact on encryption. He has accused some critics, including Big Tech companies, of spreading misinformation about the bill.

"Bill C-22 does not authorize indiscriminate surveillance and does not permit or compel companies to introduce systemic vulnerabilities or so-called 'backdoors.' Any claims suggesting otherwise are incorrect," Simon Lafortune, the minister's spokesperson, said in a statement.

Apple said in a statement it appreciates the Canadian government's efforts to improve the bill, but the current version would still undermine the company's ability to offer privacy and security features, including encryption, "even as AI and other evolving technologies provide hackers with new tools to exploit cybersecurity weaknesses."

US lawmakers have also pushed back. In May, Republican House Representatives Jim Jordan and Brian Mast warned in a letter to Anandasangaree that the bill would "create significant cross-border risks to the security and data privacy of Americans."

The Canadian Senate committee is the bill's last legislative hurdle before potential passage into law. While the appointed chamber rarely rejects bills outright, it frequently secures amendments — leaving tech giants and privacy advocates one last venue to lobby for changes.

article_content_zh:
周一，2026年11月16日格林威治标准时间凌晨3点（彭博社）-总理马克·卡尼（Mark Carney）的政府正面临大型科技公司对安全立法的强烈反对，该立法将要求公司保留并将用户数据交给执法部门。

Meta Platforms Inc.、Apple Inc. 和 Alphabet Inc. 的游说者和高管正在渥太华发动最后的闪电战，以便在法案通过之前重写该法案。周一，Meta、Signal Messenger LLC 和 Tailscale Inc. 的领导人将在参议院委员会的一次重要听证会上进行斗争，该听证会将形成立法的最终形式。

C-22 法案，即所谓的“合法访问”立法，旨在允许加拿大间谍机构和警察部门强制电子服务提供商保存和移交某些元数据。政府坚称这些措施只是让加拿大与其五眼联盟和七国集团盟友保持一致。

科技公司、隐私倡导者和美国立法者反驳说，该法案远远超出了加拿大同行采用的框架，警告称它将威胁平台安全和用户隐私。 Meta 辩称，该法律将有效地将其平台征召为“政府监控机构的一个部门”。

Meta 加拿大公共政策主管 Rachel Curran 在接受采访时表示：“这些系统的加拿大用户的安全和隐私确实有可能受到损害。”

对于卡尼政府来说，这场战斗可能会导致科技投资降温，与美国的紧张关系升级，并将注重隐私的平台赶出加拿大市场。 Signal威胁称，如果该法案以目前的形式通过，他将退出加拿大。瑞士科技公司 Proton AG 表示将重新考虑在该国的扩张计划。

该法案的批评者反对一项规定，该规定允许政府强制电子服务提供商将某些用户元数据保留最多六个月，以便在需要时向执法官员披露。

拟议的法律还可能迫使一些公司解锁加密数据——但前提是他们建立了加密技术并拥有解锁所需的信息。今年早些时候，立法者修改了该法案，明确表示公司也不能被迫在其软件中引入“系统漏洞”。

这些护栏旨在缓解 Signal 和 WhatsApp 母公司 Meta 等公司对该法案针对端到端加密的担忧。这种形式的加密确保只有发送者和接收者可以读取消息，这意味着该公司没有能力解密它们。

即便如此，隐私倡导者和技术领袖认为，该法案仍然赋予政府广泛的权力，可以命令企业建立“技术能力”来拦截通信和移交数据。

科技公司长期以来一直警告说，他们不能在不削弱所有用户安全的情况下仅为执法部门创建“后门”访问。 Curran 表示，一项会让 Meta 的系统更容易受到攻击的命令对该公司来说是一条“红线”，也可能是其行业同行的一条“红线”。

她说：“这可能会让加拿大处于服务提供商和政府之间最终陷入僵局的境地，这对加拿大人不利。”

去年，英国和苹果公司也面临着类似的纠纷，当时政府命令该公司规避该公司用于保护存储在其云服务上的用户数据的加密技术。苹果对该命令提出质疑，并取消了针对英国用户的高级数据保护功能。此案仍在法庭审理中。

“在假设的未来，如果我们面临类似的订单，我们将不得不考虑这些选择，”柯兰说。

公共安全部长加里·阿南达桑加里 (Gary Anandasangaree) 表示，该法案已经过修改，以缓解英国苹果公司对加密技术潜在影响的担忧。他指责包括大型科技公司在内的一些批评者散布有关该法案的错误信息。

“C-22 法案并未授权不分皂白的监视，也不允许或强迫公司引入系统漏洞或所谓的‘后门’。任何其他暗示的说法都是不正确的，”部长发言人西蒙·拉福图恩 (Simon Lafortune) 在一份声明中表示。

苹果在一份声明中表示，它赞赏加拿大政府为改进该法案所做的努力，但当前版本仍然会削弱该公司提供包括加密在内的隐私和安全功能的能力，“即使人工智能和其他不断发展的技术为黑客提供了利用网络安全弱点的新工具。”

美国立法者也予以反击。今年 5 月，共和党众议院代表吉姆·乔丹 (Jim Jordan) 和布莱恩·马斯特 (Brian Mast) 在致 Anandasangaree 的一封信中警告称，该法案将“对美国人的安全和数据隐私造成重大跨境风险”。

加拿大参议院委员会是该法案在可能成为法律之前的最后一个立法障碍。虽然指定的议院很少彻底拒绝法案，但它经常会获得修正案——这让科技巨头和隐私倡导者成为游说变革的最后场所。

article_content:
How more than 1,800 scientists used ChatGPT—and what they expect AI to mean for scientific discovery. Explore the findings in our new report.

Scientific progress depends on researchers asking new questions and finding ways to answer them. AI is becoming part of that work, but we’re still learning where it helps and what it could mean for discovery.

OpenAI’s Economic Research team studied more than 580,000 scientific messages from 1,819 scientists in the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers summer pilot and surveyed 251 participants.

Scientists used ChatGPT across the research process, from reviewing literature to analyzing evidence and developing ideas. Surveyed participants estimated that the same work, at the same quality, would have taken 1.9 times as long without AI. And 98% of those who answered our question about discovery timelines expected AI to accelerate discovery in their field.

By default, OpenAI does not use participants’ data from the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to train its models. To protect researchers’ privacy, we used tools called automated classifiers to sort messages by the type of research activity, such as reviewing literature, writing code, or analyzing data. The research team could see those categories, but did not read the underlying messages or ChatGPT’s responses.

### AI is part of scientists’ daily work

We studied how scientists used ChatGPT across the research process.

### 68% of scientists used ChatGPT to develop research ideas

We looked at how scientists used ChatGPT for ideation. The figures below describe their messages about research ideas.

of the time, scientists brought a specific question for ChatGPT to work with.

of the time, scientists brought an idea and asked ChatGPT to refine it.

of the time, scientists asked ChatGPT to suggest a research question.

The message could not be categorized into one of the other activities.

### 98% of surveyed scientists expect AI to speed up discovery in their field.

We asked scientists across different fields to imagine a discovery that would take 10 years without AI and estimate how long it would take with AI.

### Scientists stay involved even after delegating tasks to ChatGPT

We measured how often scientists followed up to clarify, check, or revise ChatGPT’s responses across different research activities.

### How could AI further scientific progress?

We asked scientists who expected faster discovery to explain why. Three reasons stood out in their answers.

Get research done faster

Find more promising research questions

Pursue a wider range of questions

Scientists could give multiple reasons. Percentages show the share of all 367 reasons identified in 224 written responses.

### Looking ahead

Scientists in this study used ChatGPT to explore ideas, analyze evidence, write code, and communicate their findings. Their responses also point to ambitions beyond saving time: finding more promising questions and pursuing a wider range of research.

Understanding whether those expectations translate into faster discovery will take more research. Progress will also depend on the funding, staff, and experimental capacity scientists need to test their ideas.

We want to empower more scientists to explore what AI can make possible in their work. Alongside this research, we’re expanding ChatGPT for Academic Researchers, with free access for more than 200,000 researchers around the world. Helping scientists turn their ideas into discoveries that improve lives is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

For more on this study, read the complete paper or download the key findings.

“Tools like ChatGPT are helping us accelerate scientific discovery. It’s really a playground for a scientist like myself.”

前沿科学：科学家如何使用 ChatGPT。 超过 1,800 名科学家如何使用 ChatGPT，以及他们期望 AI 对科学发现意味着什么。探索我们新报告中的发现。

科学进步取决于研究人员提出新问题并找到答案的方法。人工智能正在成为这项工作的一部分，但我们仍在了解它在哪里有帮助以及它对发现意味着什么。
ai_analysis.digest_en:
How more than 1,800 scientists used ChatGPT—and what they expect AI to mean for scientific discovery. Explore the findings in our new report.

Scientific progress depends on researchers asking new questions and finding ways to answer them. AI is becoming part of that work, but we’re still learning where it helps and what it could mean for discovery.

OpenAI’s Economic Research team studied more than 580,000 scientific messages from 1,819 scientists in the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers summer
key_points_zh: 核心事实：前沿科学：科学家如何使用 ChatGPT
key_points_en: Key Development: Science at the Frontier: How scientists use ChatGPT

article_content_zh:
超过 1,800 名科学家如何使用 ChatGPT，以及他们期望 AI 对科学发现意味着什么。探索我们新报告中的发现。

科学进步取决于研究人员提出新问题并找到答案的方法。人工智能正在成为这项工作的一部分，但我们仍在了解它在哪里有帮助以及它对发现意味着什么。

OpenAI 的经济研究团队研究了 ChatGPT 学术研究人员夏季试点项目中来自 1,819 名科学家的 580,000 多条科学信息，并对 251 名参与者进行了调查。

科学家们在整个研究过程中使用 ChatGPT，从审查文献到分析证据和发展想法。接受调查的参与者估计，如果没有人工智能，同样的工作、同样的质量，需要的时间会是原来的 1.9 倍。在回答我们有关发现时间表问题的人中，98% 预计人工智能将加速其领域的发现。

默认情况下，OpenAI 不会使用来自 ChatGPT 学术研究人员计划的参与者数据来训练其模型。为了保护研究人员的隐私，我们使用称为自动分类器的工具根据研究活动的类型对消息进行排序，例如审查文献、编写代码或分析数据。研究团队可以看到这些类别，但没有阅读底层消息或 ChatGPT 的响应。

### 人工智能是科学家日常工作的一部分

我们研究了科学家如何在整个研究过程中使用 ChatGPT。

### 68% 的科学家使用 ChatGPT 来开发研究想法

我们研究了科学家们是如何使用ChatGPT进行创意的。下面的图表描述了他们关于研究想法的信息。

当时，科学家们给ChatGPT带来了一个具体的问题。

当时，科学家们带来了一个想法，并要求ChatGPT对其进行改进。

当时，科学家们请ChatGPT提出一个研究问题。

该消息无法归类为其他活动之一。

### 98% 的受访科学家预计人工智能将加速其领域的发现。

我们请不同领域的科学家想象一下，如果没有人工智能，一项发现需要 10 年时间，并估计使用人工智能需要多长时间。

### 即使在将任务委托给 ChatGPT 后，科学家们仍然参与其中

我们测量了科学家在不同研究活动中跟进澄清、检查或修改 ChatGPT 响应的频率。

### 人工智能如何推动科学进步？

我们请那些期待更快发现的科学家解释原因。他们的回答中突出了三个原因。

寻找更多有前途的研究问题

科学家可以给出多种原因。百分比显示了224份书面回复中确定的所有367个原因所占的比例。

这项研究中的科学家使用 ChatGPT 来探索想法、分析证据、编写代码并交流他们的发现。他们的回答还表明了超越节省时间的雄心：寻找更有希望的问题并进行更广泛的研究。

了解这些期望是否会转化为更快的发现需要更多的研究。进展还取决于科学家测试其想法所需的资金、人员和实验能力。

我们希望让更多的科学家能够探索人工智能在他们的工作中可以发挥什么作用。除了这项研究之外，我们还在为学术研究人员扩展 ChatGPT，为全球超过 200,000 名研究人员提供免费访问。帮助科学家将他们的想法转化为改善生活的发现是我们确保 AGI 造福全人类的使命的核心。

有关这项研究的更多信息，请阅读完整论文或下载主要发现。

“像 ChatGPT 这样的工具正在帮助我们加速科学发现。对于像我这样的科学家来说，这确实是一个游乐场。”

title: An interview with Rockstar executives at the company's Edinburgh HQ about GTA VI, encouraging players to avoid rampages, realism, building the game, and more (Keza MacDonald/The Guardian)

author: The Guardian
article_content:
It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat.

The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness.

One month before release, it is quiet at Rockstar’s headquarters. A lot of people have finished their labour on the game and are taking time off in the run-up to launch – a well-deserved rest after more than 10 years of development. Those who remain here are caught in the strange no man’s land between finishing a piece of art and releasing it into the world. When it does come out, GTA VI is expected to be the most profitable piece of entertainment ever made, projected to shift tens of millions of copies and earn billions in its first year; its predecessor, 2013’s GTA V, sold 230m copies. In the midst of a horrible time for the games business, full of studio closures layoffs and soaring development costs, a whole industry is relying on GTA VI to give it a shot in the arm. On one near-deserted floor, a screen shows a countdown to the release date.

For many players, meanwhile, the 13-year wait for a new Grand Theft Auto has become unbearable. When footage of GTA VI made its glitzy premiere on Netflix, it almost took the streaming giant’s servers down. Its first trailer has been viewed 300m times on YouTube alone. Across the world, people have booked days off work on 19 November to experience this event together – one of those increasingly rare shared global cultural moments in an age when we all live in our own algorithmic content bubbles.

There is a slightly strained atmosphere at Rockstar North, and not just because of the pressure of GTA VI’s impending release. Over in Glasgow, Rockstar is also defending a high-profile employment tribunal case over the dismissal of 34 of its employees last year, who claim they were fired because they were involved in union organisation efforts. The case was due to wind up in October, but will now drag on right up to Grand Theft Auto VI’s release. A few days before my visit, head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe was testifying in court as former employees and their reps at the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB) protested outside.

n $1bn making. On screen, Jason and Lucia – two young criminals on the run – are on their way from a bar to a nightclub, walking through downtown Vice City as the last vestiges of sunlight disappear and the streets become bathed in fluorescence. He is tall, square-shouldered, in a T-shirt and shorts; she has her hair up in a ponytail, wearing one of those merciless long-sleeved crop tops that almost nobody can pull off.

After dancing with each other at the club, part of a crowded mass of virtual people gyrating in neon UV-reactive mesh tops, they will each don a cap, sunglasses and a bandana over the face, and hold up a jewellery store before escaping into the night in a beaten-up car, the boot stuffed with holdalls filled with cash and sizeable firearms, evading the cops by driving right through a cornfield in an apt echo of Bonnie and Clyde.

Lucia is the first woman to have headline billing in a GTA game, part of a long lineage of criminal protagonists who range from the straightforwardly psychopathic (GTA V’s Trevor) to the unexpectedly sympathetic (GTA IV’s Niko Bellic, and San Andreas’s CJ). GTA VI is both her story and Jason’s. For some acts of this game you are locked into one character’s perspective, but most of the time you can switch freely between them. When they are apart, you can ensure they text and call each other. When they’re together, you can take them on little dates: to the gym, out to a bar, to a meditation retreat or to a liquor-store stick-up. You as the player become the steward of their relationship, and if you neglect it then there will be consequences. “You’re dropped into their lives,” Nelson explains, as Lucia speeds along a highway, Jason leaning out of the window to shoot at the tyres of the cop car pursuing them. “The relationship is yours to nurture or yours to lose. Whether it remains a romantic relationship is in your hands.”

This dynamic is not merely interesting – it is transformational for Grand Theft Auto. The series made its name on black humour and directionless violent mayhem, setting players free in virtual pastiches of New York, Miami or Los Angeles to crash stolen cars and terrorise pedestrians. GTA V in particular was an extravagant equal-opportunity offender, taking aim at everyone and everything from the US government to narcissistic tech bros, spoilt LA brats to hillbillies, the ultra-rich to caravan-dwelling wasters. Nobody has ever cared about anybody very much in a GTA game. Here, though, we are being asked not just to care about these characters, but to act out how they care for each other. When they are together, you can press a button to make them hold hands.

It is faintly unbelievable to see this game in action after it has existed for so long only as fervent rumour. GTA VI has been in development in some form since 2015, when the team took their first research trips to Miami (at this time, the game’s codename was Project Americas, reflecting a later abandoned ambition to set it across two continents). But it was only announced in December 2023, and has been delayed twice since. I get the impression that the people at Rockstar have basically been forced to put their metaphorical paintbrushes down. “They would never stop working on this game if they had the choice,” Kolbe says, somewhat ruefully. “It’s really hard to close it down,” Nelson admits. “If you step away and get a little bit of space from it, you can look at it objectively and go: ‘I’m proud of what we’ve done’. But ultimately, it is being taken away from you, and you do the best you can to finish it in the time that you’re told.”

Usually when shown a video game ahead of release, one is taken through a highly choreographed slice of the action designed to show it at its best, but that’s not what’s happening here. We’re simply tooling about in a densely populated Vice City, and almost anything I suggest, we can do. Walking out from Jason and Lucia’s flamingo-wallpapered apartment into the Florida sunshine, the first thing we see is a woman walking a dog. I ask if we can pet it; Nelson presses a button and Jason says: “Is it cool if I pet your dog?” “Course, she loves to greet her public,” the woman replies, before Jason stoops to give the pup a fuss. You can overhear pedestrians’ conversations as you pass by, and interrupting them might result in a bemused “Have we met?” or a stream of invective. Later, I see a gull sitting on a post by the beach and ask, just to be annoying, what kind of bird it is. Jason pulls out a pair of binoculars, the gull is recorded in a wildlife logbook, and I am told with pride that there are 62 types of birds to spot.

n’t just steal any car or bust their way into a bank; at the start they can only hotwire low-end vehicles and pick basic locks, working their way up to the higher-value jobs later. “These guys are a younger couple with their backs against the wall,” Nelson says. “Narratively, it doesn’t make a lot of sense for them to go out and cause as much carnage and make as much noise as they can.” Instead of whipping out an assault rifle in the middle of a crowded street and sending everyone scattering, you have to scope out your targets, whether it’s a gas station or an upscale mall boutique. You can disable security cameras or steal the footage, find back doors and safe codes so that you can get in without pulling a gun on anyone, and get out before witnesses arrive.

Fail to do these things and chaos ramps up quickly. After a couple of small-time crime sprees, we take Jason and Lucia to a well-protected jewellery store, where Lucia turns her pistol on the security guards for a few tense seconds before they surrender. Upstairs, though, where Jason is shoving money from the safe into a holdall, another guard decides to shoot rather than surrender. A desperate scramble ensues, in which Jason smacks the guy with the butt of a gun to knock him out while Lucia yells from the front of the store, and as they climb on to a stolen motorbike to make their getaway, the police arrive. The chase takes us halfway around the district, followed by cop cars and helicopters. When they eventually make it back to their car, Jason and Lucia stow the cash, change their clothes, and lie low in the outskirts of the city for a while to wait out the heat.

GTA VI is still very much a game about crime and criminals, but it strongly encourages you towards playing in-character and avoiding directionless rampages. In this way it is heavily inspired by Rockstar’s Red Dead Redemption 2 (2018), in which you play an outlaw in the old west who comes to regret his life of violence. For Nelson, one of the greatest challenges of GTA VI’s development has been figuring out how to encourage players to behave differently without restricting their freedom, which would be antithetical to Rockstar’s creative philosophy. Even with an unlimited budget, you can’t solve the central tension of the form: the balance between the story that developers are trying to tell, and the random whims of any given player.

f 2002’s GTA Vice City, VI’s spiritual predecessor, over its depictions of violence against those groups. US courts have consistently upheld Rockstar’s first amendment rights, but this history hints at a cultural double standard. It is widely accepted that film and TV can depict violence without endorsing it – few would seriously venture that Breaking Bad endorses cooking meth – but when it comes to video games, where the player takes an active role, they are often seen to be lionising the behaviour they depict.

As video game graphics have got more realistic – it is hard to see, in retrospect, how the now comically low-resolution puppet characters of 00s GTA games provoked such outrage – Grand Theft Auto has sought to contextualise its violence. Its cinematic storytelling and character development ambitions have grown exponentially, as have its budget and team size, which has quadrupled since GTA V. The entire history of games is a story of talented technical and creative people finding ways to work around technological constraints and make things that were never possible before, working magic with blocky characters and limited graphical power. But now the limitations that defined the scope of previous GTA games are essentially gone. The leash is off.

“What we have grappled with is the transition from being limited by technical constraints to being limited by human resource constraints,” Nelson says. “Like, how much can we physically build? You can keep going for ever … People say you can throw money at the problem, and you can to an extent, but it’s no guarantee of making something good.”

It’s true that with all that time, effort and money, Rockstar has been able to achieve a level of detail in GTA VI that is beyond anything I’ve ever seen in a game – even beyond Red Dead Redemption 2, which was so extravagantly, naturalistically detailed that someone went to the trouble of modelling horse testicles that retract in cold weather. In a GTA VI gas station, Nelson takes evident pleasure in showing me detailed eating and drinking animations as Jason wanders around with a doughnut in one hand and a six-pack of beer in the other – the liquid inside the bottles sloshes realistically as he walks, and the racks are stocked with fully illustrated magazines that you can take off the shelf and read through. Every one of the pedestrians you see outside has been designed by someone, even down to their clothes.

Why go to this trouble? In the PlayStation 2 era, Rockstar was releasing a new GTA game every couple of years; they weren’t radically different from one another in terms of gameplay, but their shifting settings and characters allowed the series’ makers to stretch their creative muscles. By contrast, it’s now been 13 years and two console generations since the last GTA. Why spend all this time on a single, ostentatiously gigantic project? It comes down to this, Nelson says: if you were a developer with these resources, the only developer with these resources, wouldn’t you go for the most ambitious thing you could?

“They could have made GTA 5.5, and done it faster,” says Kolbe. “Ultimately, that’s not what they wanted.”

Nelson nods: “You have to take big swings. It can’t be just more of the same.”

Grand Theft Auto VI is released for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on 19 November.

article_content_zh:
踏上它……侠盗猎车手 VI 即将呼啸进城。插图：Matt Taylor/The Guardian 全屏查看图片 踏上它……侠盗猎车手 VI 即将呼啸进城。插图：Matt Taylor/卫报 十年、数千名员工和十亿美元：《侠盗猎车手 VI》的独家内幕故事史诗犯罪传奇的最新一期终于来了。我们访问 Rockstar Games，亲身体验这十年来的文化盛事 – 并可以证实它的真实性，而不是像宣传的那样

许多人仍然感到惊讶的是，侠盗猎车手是一款明目张胆的美国犯罪系列游戏，过去 20 年来一直是世界上最受欢迎和最具争议的视频游戏之一，但它主要是在苏格兰制作的。但如果你在爱丁堡长大，开发商 Rockstar North 就是这个地方背景神话的一部分。在 2000 年代的某个时候，很多人作为游戏测试人员或员工都曾来过这个工作室。当时作为爱丁堡的一名学生，我经常听到高管家里举办疯狂派对的传闻，就像游戏中的那样颓废。在酒吧、生日或乔迁庆典上，你可能会遇到一个人，他声称自己想出了一种幼稚的双关语，为游戏内的生意增色不少（例如日本餐厅 Nutsaki 或炸鸡连锁店 Cluckin' Bell）。 《侠盗猎车手》现在是由全球近 5000 人的庞大团队制作的，但它的中枢神经系统仍然在荷里路德，在亚瑟王宝座的阴影下。

最新的侠盗猎车手游戏的背景确实离苏格兰首都不远了。侠盗猎车手 6 将我们带到列奥尼达州的罪恶城，这是对佛罗里达州迈阿密的模仿。这是一座霓虹灯笼罩的大都市，充满了肮脏和斗争，过度的狂欢派对与几乎不被掩盖的黑社会和不可预测的佛罗里达疯狂并存。

距离发售还有一个月，Rockstar 总部一片安静。许多人已经完成了这款游戏的工作，并在发布前准备休息——经过 10 多年的开发，这是当之无愧的休息。那些留在这里的人在完成一件艺术品和将其发布到世界之间时陷入了奇怪的无人区。当《GTA VI》问世时，预计将成为有史以来最赚钱的娱乐作品，预计第一年销量将达到数千万份，收入达数十亿美元；它的前身，2013 年的 GTA V，售出了 2.3 亿份。在游戏行业面临着一个可怕的时期，工作室倒闭、裁员和开发成本飙升的情况下，整个行业都在依靠《GTA VI》来打一剂强心剂。在一个几乎空无一人的楼层，屏幕上显示着发布日期的倒计时。

与此同时，对于许多玩家来说，等待新侠盗猎车手 13 年已经变得难以忍受。当 GTA VI 的片段在 N​​etflix 上精彩首映时，这家流媒体巨头的服务器几乎瘫痪了。仅在 YouTube 上，其第一部预告片的观看次数就已达 3 亿次。世界各地的人们都预订了 11 月 19 日的休息日，共同体验这一活动——在我们都生活在自己的算法内容泡沫的时代，这是越来越罕见的共享全球文化时刻之一。

Rockstar North 的气氛有些紧张，这不仅仅是因为即将发布的 GTA VI 的压力。在格拉斯哥，Rockstar 还在为一起备受瞩目的就业法庭案件进行辩护，该案件涉及去年解雇 34 名员工的事件，这些员工声称自己因参与工会组织活动而被解雇。该案原定于 10 月份结束，但现在将一直拖到《侠盗猎车手 VI》发布为止。在我访问的前几天，出版主管詹妮弗·科尔贝 (Jennifer Kolbe) 正在法庭上作证，而英国独立工人联盟 (IWGB) 的前雇员及其代表则在法庭外抗议。

在俱乐部里，一群穿着霓虹灯紫外线反应网状上衣旋转的虚拟人物中，彼此跳舞后，他们每个人都会戴上帽子，戴上墨镜，在脸上戴上头巾，举起一家珠宝店，然后开着一辆破旧的汽车逃入夜色，后备箱里塞满了装满现金和大型枪支的旅行袋，开车穿过玉米地躲避警察，这恰如其分地呼应了《邦妮和克莱德》。

露西娅是第一个在 GTA 游戏中登上头条的女性，她是众多犯罪主角中的一员，这些主角的范围从直率的精神变态者（GTA V 的 Trevor）到出人意料的同情心（GTA IV 的 Niko Bellic 和 San Andreas 的 CJ）。 《GTA VI》既是她的故事，也是杰森的故事。对于这款游戏的某些行为，你会被锁定在一个角色的视角中，但大多数时候你可以在它们之间自由切换。当他们分开时，您可以确保他们互相发短信和打电话。当他们在一起时，你可以带他们进行一些小约会：去健身房、去酒吧、去冥想静修处或去酒类商店。作为玩家，你成为他们关系的管理者，如果你忽视了这一点，就会产生后果。 “你融入了他们的生活，”尼尔森解释道，露西娅在高速公路上飞驰，杰森探出窗外，向追赶他们的警车的轮胎开枪。 “这种关系是由你来培养的，还是由你来失去的。是否仍然是一段浪漫的关系取决于你自己。”

这种动态不仅有趣，而且对侠盗猎车手来说也是变革性的。该系列以黑色幽默和无方向的暴力混乱而闻名，让玩家在纽约、迈阿密或洛杉矶的虚拟模仿中自由地撞毁被盗的汽车并恐吓行人。 《侠盗猎车手 V》尤其是一个奢侈的平等机会犯罪者，它的目标是所有人和一切，从美国政府到自恋的科技兄弟，从被宠坏的洛杉矶小孩到乡下人，从超级富豪到住在大篷车里的浪费者。在 GTA 游戏中，没有人非常关心任何人。然而，在这里，我们不仅被要求关心这些角色，还要表现出他们如何互相关心。当他们在一起时，你可以按一个按钮让他们牵手。

这款游戏已经存在这么久了，仅仅只是热切的谣言，但现在看到这款游戏的实际运作，实在令人难以置信。自 2015 年以来，《GTA VI》一直在以某种形式进行开发，当时团队首次前往迈阿密进行考察（当时，游戏的代号是“美洲计划”，反映了后来放弃的跨越两大洲的雄心）。但直到 2023 年 12 月才宣布，此后已两次推迟。我的印象是，Rockstar 的人基本上被迫放下了他们的隐喻画笔。 “如果有选择的话，他们永远不会停止开发这款游戏，”科尔贝有些遗憾地说道。 “关闭它真的很难，”尼尔森承认。 “如果你离开并从中获得一点空间，你就可以客观地看待它并说：‘我为我们所做的事情感到自豪’。但最终，它会被从你身边夺走，你会尽最大努力在被告知的时间内完成它。”

通常，在发布之前播放视频游戏时，人们会看到精心设计的动作片段，旨在展示游戏的最佳状态，但这不是这里发生的情况。我们只是在人口稠密的罪恶都市里闲逛，几乎我建议的任何事情我们都能做到。从杰森和露西亚的火烈鸟壁纸公寓走出，走进佛罗里达州的阳光下，我们首先看到的是一个遛狗的女人。我问我们是否可以抚摸它；尼尔森按下按钮，杰森说：“我抚摸你的狗很酷吗？” “当然，她喜欢向公众打招呼，”这位女士回答道，然后杰森弯下腰去惹这只小狗。当你经过时，你可以无意中听到行人的谈话，打断他们可能会导致困惑“我们见过吗？”或一连串谩骂。后来，我看到一只海鸥坐在海滩边的柱子上，为了惹恼我，我就问它是什么鸟。 Jason 拿出一副双筒望远镜，海鸥被记录在野生动物日志中，我自豪地得知有 62 种鸟类可供观赏。

如果不做这些事情，混乱就会迅速加剧。在发生了几次小规模的犯罪事件后，我们带杰森和露西娅去了一家戒备森严的珠宝店，露西娅在那里用手枪指着保安，紧张了几秒钟，然后他们投降了。然而，在楼上，杰森正把保险箱里的钱塞进手提包里，另一名警卫决定开枪而不是投降。随后发生了一场绝望的争夺，杰森用枪托打了那个人，把他打晕了，而露西娅在商店前面大喊大叫，当他们爬上一辆偷来的摩托车逃跑时，警察赶到了。追捕行动绕了半个街区，警车和直升机紧随其后。当杰森和露西娅最终回到车上时，他们把现金存起来，换了衣服，在市郊躺了一会儿，等待炎热的天气过去。

title: In a Sloppified A.I. World, Only Humans Can Build ‘Ecosystems’
title_en: In a Sloppified A.I. World, Only Humans Can Build ‘Ecosystems’
author: Lora Kelley
article_content:
Networking has long been crucial in tech, an industry where so-called warm intros, founder dinners and alumni communities are central to the culture (and to deal making).

But lately, start-ups and venture capital firms have been sharpening their focus on human connection, by hiring people for “ecosystem” jobs. Such roles, which have titles like “start-up ecosystem lead” or “ecosystem growth manager,” focus on building or maintaining relationships among various parties on a company’s behalf. In this way, the people ushering in the artificial intelligence revolution are doubling down on in-person ties.

The workers in such roles often spend their days planning events, orchestrating partnerships, supporting clients and leading trainings. Are the tasks new? Not really. But the framing is.

“When companies talk about ecosystem, they are talking about trying to cultivate and tend to an extended network — not just of customers but also of partners, distribution channels, supporters and advocates,” said Yoni Rechtman, a partner at Slow Ventures, a venture capital firm.

The venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz defined ecosystem as “the bottom-up vector of trust in venture,” and the firm’s “ecosystem lead” explained his role as “focused on expanding and reinforcing the multitude of networks spanning our firm.”

Ecosystem roles exist on various teams, including marketing, partnerships and sales, and the job’s specifics vary from company to company, said Natalie Sportelli, who since January has held the title “start-up ecosystem” at Clay, an A.I. sales tool start-up. In recent months, her projects have included putting together product demonstrations for a partner’s portfolio companies, coordinating product coaching sessions with customers and collaborating with other start-up program leaders for a panel in London about building A.I.-native sales organizations.

“We’re not just trying to sell — we’re trying to create programming that makes start-ups successful,” she said.

Though the role is still niche, the rate of job titles with “ecosystem” in them quadrupled on LinkedIn from 2010 to 2025, according to Nick Bloom and Gideon Slocum Moore, researchers at Stanford who have analyzed job-title data on the platform. (Only a small share of new “ecosystem” roles in recent years, they noted, appear related to the field of ecology.)

People in tech have dropped the phrase ecosystem for as long as Mr. Rechtman can remember — referring to the “tech ecosystem” and the “start-up ecosystem” — but its presence in job titles is a more recent development, he said. Ms. Sportelli, too, has noticed an uptick in such roles in the past year, which she attributes partly to a hunger for connection brought on by the rise of A.I. Lately, there is a “premium on in-person,” including events, she said.

The bet is that people beget interest from other people.

“It’s very difficult to stand out in a sloppified feed and a sloppified inbox,” Mr. Rechtman said, referring to A.I. slop. In a world where companies can easily blast potential customers with A.I.-generated content all day, he added, “getting attention is much harder, and you need to be more creative in how you meet people and build relationships with them.”

A wave of new A.I. tools also means a wave of new stakeholders and relationships to manage.

“People now have a ton of vendors, and those vendors all need to work together — and the relationships between them are more complicated,” Mr. Rechtman said.

The A.I. era has spawned a number of new job functions — with trendy new titles to go with them.

“There are some roles that come into vogue because they sound cool or because you feel like you’re investing in the right things by hiring for them,” Ms. Sportelli said. “Start-up and venture people love a good branding moment when it comes to job titles.”

article_content_zh:
长期以来，网络在科技行业一直至关重要，在这个行业，所谓的热情介绍、创始人晚宴和校友社区是文化（以及交易）的核心。

但最近，初创企业和风险投资公司通过雇用人员从事“生态系统”工作，加强了对人际关系的关注。这些职位的头衔包括“初创生态系统领导者”或“生态系统增长经理”，重点是代表公司建立或维护各方之间的关系。通过这种方式，引领人工智能革命的人们正在加倍加强面对面的联系。

担任此类职务的员工经常花时间规划活动、协调合作伙伴关系、支持客户和领导培训。任务是新的吗？并不真地。但框架是。

风险投资公司 Slow Ventures 的合伙人 Yoni Rechtman 表示：“当公司谈论生态系统时，他们谈论的是努力培养和维护一个扩展的网络——不仅是客户的网络，还包括合作伙伴、分销渠道、支持者和倡导者的网络。”

风险投资公司Andreessen Horowitz将生态系统定义为“自下而上的风险信任向量”，该公司的“生态系统负责人”将自己的职责解释为“专注于拓展和强化覆盖我们公司的众多网络”。

Natalie Sportelli表示，生态系统角色存在于各个团队中，包括营销、合作伙伴关系和销售团队，而且该岗位的具体职责因公司而异。自1月起，她在人工智能销售工具初创公司Clay担任“初创企业生态系统”一职。

斯坦福大学研究人员尼克·布鲁姆 (Nick Bloom) 和吉迪恩·斯洛库姆·摩尔 (Gideon Slocum Moore) 对 LinkedIn 平台上的职位数据进行了分析，他们表示，虽然这个职位仍然属于小众市场，但从 2010 年到 2025 年，LinkedIn 上包含“生态系统”的职位名称比例翻了两番。 （他们指出，近年来新的“生态系统”角色中只有一小部分似乎与生态领域有关。）

从雷希特曼先生记事起，科技界人士就已经放弃了“生态系统”这个词——指的是“科技生态系统”和“初创生态系统”——但他说，这个词出现在职位名称中是最近才出现的。斯波特利女士也注意到，过去一年中此类角色有所增加，她将其部分归因于人工智能的兴起带来的对联系的渴望。她说，最近，“面对面的交流越来越多”，包括活动。

赌注是人们会引起其他人的兴趣。

“要在杂乱的信息流和杂乱的收件箱中脱颖而出是非常困难的，”雷希特曼先生说，他指的是人工智能。斜坡。他补充说，在当今的世界里，公司可以轻松地用人工智能生成的内容来吸引潜在客户，“获得关注要困难得多，你需要在与人们见面并与他们建立关系的方式上更具创造性。”

新的人工智能浪潮工具还意味着需要管理一波新的利益相关者和关系。

“人们现在有大量的供应商，而这些供应商都需要共同合作——而且他们之间的关系更加复杂，”雷希特曼先生说。

人工智能这个时代催生了许多新的工作职能——随之而来的是流行的新头衔。

“有些职位之所以流行，是因为它们听起来很酷，或者是因为你觉得通过雇用这些职位，你是在投资正确的事情，”斯波特利女士说。 “初创企业和风险投资人士喜欢在职位名称方面树立良好的品牌形象。”

title: The Backyard Battle Over Amazon Delivery Drones ‘Stealing the Sky’
title_en: The Backyard Battle Over Amazon Delivery Drones ‘Stealing the Sky’
